name: Notion
summary: Reaching public launch is mostly self-serve. You create a public connection in Notion's Developer portal, get an OAuth client ID and secret, and Notion's docs say the connection works through OAuth without a Marketplace listing. The only formal review is the optional Marketplace listing, which takes 5–10 business days. One line in the docs (the authorization URL field fills in after you submit for review) means you should check in the portal whether submitting is needed before outside workspaces can install.
tierReason: Notion's docs say public connections work independently of Marketplace listings, so OAuth installs don't depend on the reviewed listing. Confidence is medium because of the wording about submitting for review.

composio.note: Composio has a managed Notion OAuth app, so you can prototype before you create your own public connection. Register your own before launch so your connection name and logo appear on Notion's consent screen. The separate NOTION_MCP toolkit requires your own OAuth app.

stages.name: Your workspace
stages.whoCanConnect: You, from your development workspace or any workspace you selected
stages.userSees: Notion's consent screen with your connection name, the capabilities it asks for, and a page picker
stages.unlock: Create the connection with the 'Any workspace' installation scope. If the portal asks you to, submit it so the authorization URL fills in.

stages.name: Public launch
stages.whoCanConnect: Any Notion user who has full access to the pages they share. Connections set to 'Selected workspaces only' stay limited to the workspaces you chose.
stages.userSees: The same consent screen and page picker. A Marketplace listing is optional and only changes whether users can find you in Notion.

requirements.label: A Notion workspace you own
requirements.detail: Notion requires workspace ownership to create internal connections. StackOne reports the same for public connections.

requirements.label: Your OAuth redirect URI
requirements.detail: You must enter at least one redirect URI when you create the connection.

requirements.label: Connection logo
requirements.detail: StackOne's setup guide marks the logo as required on the creation form.

requirements.label: Marketplace listing assets (optional)
requirements.detail: Only needed if you want to appear in the Marketplace: a name, description, category, tags, images and a logo.

steps.title: Open Public connections in the Developer portal
steps.detail: Sign in to Notion as a workspace owner, open the Developer portal and choose Public connections under Build.
actions: Go to app.notion.com/developers/connections
In the sidebar, choose Build > Public connections
steps.agentNote: Once you're signed in, an agent can do the rest of the form.

steps.title: Create the public connection
steps.detail: Click Create new connection. Enter the name, development workspace, logo, your redirect URI(s) and the installation scope.
actions: Enter the connection name and pick a development workspace
Upload a logo
Add your OAuth client's redirect URI
Set Installable in to 'Any workspace' if users outside your chosen workspaces should be able to install it
steps.agentNote: An agent can fill in the form and copy in the redirect URI. You supply the logo file.
steps.gotcha: You can't change the installation scope after creation. 'Selected workspaces only' blocks other workspaces and Marketplace listing, so to switch you have to create a new connection.

steps.title: Choose content, comment and user capabilities
steps.detail: Turn on only the capabilities you need, such as reading, updating or inserting content. Turn on the capability to read user information if your app needs the user's email.
actions: Enable the content capabilities you need
Enable comment capabilities if needed
Enable 'Read user information including email addresses' if you need the email
Save
steps.gotcha: Users see these capabilities on the consent screen, so asking for more than you need can make them hesitate.

steps.title: Copy the client ID and secret into your OAuth client
steps.detail: The OAuth client ID and secret are in the Configuration tab. Store the secret outside source code.
actions: Copy the OAuth client ID
Reveal the OAuth client secret and store it in your secret manager or OAuth client
steps.agentNote: An agent can copy the client ID. You handle the client secret yourself.

steps.title: Configure your OAuth client's endpoints
steps.detail: The authorize URL is https://api.notion.com/v1/oauth/authorize with response_type=code and owner=user. The token URL is https://api.notion.com/v1/oauth/token, using HTTP Basic auth with the client ID and secret.
actions: Set the authorize URL with client_id, redirect_uri, response_type=code and owner=user
Set the token URL. Send the token request as JSON with Basic auth
Store the new refresh token after every refresh, because each refresh replaces it
steps.gotcha: Notion has no scopes parameter. Access depends on the capabilities you set and the pages the user picks. If you register more than one redirect URI, include redirect_uri in the token request.

steps.title: Connect your own workspace and test
steps.detail: Run the flow, pick some pages and confirm you get an access token, a refresh token and a workspace_id back.
steps.agentNote: An agent can drive the test while you're signed in to Notion.
steps.gotcha: The connection only sees pages the user shared in the picker. Each workspace member has to authorize it separately.

steps.title: Submit the connection if the authorization URL is empty
steps.detail: Notion's docs say the Authorization URL field fills in after a public connection is submitted for review. If the field is empty and outside users can't install, submit from the portal.
steps.agentNote: An agent can check the Configuration tab. You make the submission.
steps.gotcha: It's unclear whether this submission blocks installs or only fills in a convenience URL. You can build the authorize URL yourself from the client ID.

steps.title: Optionally submit a Marketplace listing
steps.detail: To appear in Notion's Marketplace, create a listing under Listings, link your 'Any workspace' connection and submit it. Notion replies by email within 5–10 business days.
actions: Write the name, description, category and tags
Upload images and a logo
Link the public connection and submit from Listings > Connections
steps.agentNote: An agent can draft the listing. You submit it.
steps.gotcha: Listings get rejected for brand or trademark issues and quality concerns. You can revise and resubmit.

blockers.symptom: Users from other workspaces can't install the connection
blockers.cause: The connection was created with 'Selected workspaces only', and that setting can't be changed.
blockers.fix: Create a new public connection with 'Any workspace' and switch your OAuth client to its credentials.

blockers.symptom: The Authorization URL field in the Configuration tab is blank
blockers.cause: Notion fills it in only after the public connection is submitted for review.
blockers.fix: Build the authorize URL yourself from your client ID and redirect URI, or submit the connection in the portal.

blockers.symptom: You can't create a connection
blockers.cause: You're probably not a workspace owner.
blockers.fix: Have a workspace owner create it, or create a workspace you own.

unknowns.question: Does a public connection have to be submitted or approved before users outside your workspace can authorize it?
unknowns.why: The docs say connections work without a Marketplace listing, but also that the authorization URL only fills in after submission for review. No developer reports from 2026 settle it.
unknowns.resolve: Create the connection, then authorize it from a second Notion account in a different workspace before submitting anything.

unknowns.question: Are company name, website, privacy policy, terms and support email still required?
unknowns.why: Older tutorials list these fields. The current public connections guide doesn't mention them.
unknowns.resolve: Check the live creation form in the Developer portal.

unknowns.question: How long do access tokens last?
unknowns.why: The docs describe refresh tokens but don't give an expiry.
unknowns.resolve: Look at the token response, or test how long a token keeps working.

agentCan: Fill in the public connection form and redirect URIs
Set capabilities
Copy the client ID and configure your OAuth client's endpoints
Run and check a test connection
Draft Marketplace listing text
youMust: Sign in as a Notion workspace owner
Provide the logo and handle the client secret
Choose the installation scope, which can't be changed later
Submit the connection or Marketplace listing for review

name: Calendly
summary: Calendly is self-serve. You sign up for a developer account, create a Production OAuth app with an HTTPS redirect URI and the scopes you need, and any Calendly user can connect. Calendly's docs describe no app review step.
tierReason: Calendly's docs describe creating an OAuth app in the developer console and using it at once, with no review, verification or listing step.

composio.note: Composio has a managed Calendly OAuth app, so you can prototype without registering your own. Register your own Production app before launch so your app name is on the consent screen. The separate 'Calendly MCP' toolkit needs your own app.

stages.name: Sandbox app
stages.whoCanConnect: You, plus any Calendly account you test with, through a Sandbox app that can use a localhost redirect URI.
stages.userSees: Calendly's standard consent screen showing your app name and the scopes you request.
stages.unlock: Create a second app with the Production environment and an HTTPS redirect URI.

stages.name: Production app
stages.whoCanConnect: Any Calendly user on any plan, including Free. Webhooks need a paid plan on the user's account.
stages.userSees: Calendly's standard consent screen showing your app name and the scopes you request.

requirements.label: Calendly developer account
requirements.detail: This is separate from a regular Calendly user account. You sign up at developer.calendly.com with GitHub or Google.

requirements.label: HTTPS redirect URI
requirements.detail: A Production app accepts only HTTPS redirect URIs. Sandbox apps also allow http://localhost.

requirements.label: Paid Calendly plan for webhooks (only if you use them)
requirements.detail: The connecting user's account needs a Standard, Teams or Enterprise plan before you can create webhook subscriptions. Regular GET and POST API calls work on any plan, including Free.

steps.title: Sign up for a Calendly developer account
steps.detail: At developer.calendly.com, click Sign Up in the top right and sign in with GitHub or Google. This account is separate from your Calendly user account.
actions: Open developer.calendly.com
Click Sign Up
Sign in with GitHub or Google
steps.agentNote: A person has to complete the sign-in. After that, an agent can work in the console.
steps.gotcha: Signing in to calendly.com does not give you a developer console. The developer account is separate.

steps.title: Create a Sandbox OAuth app
steps.detail: In My Apps, create an app. Set a name, Kind (Web or Native), Environment = Sandbox and your redirect URI, then select the scopes your integration needs.
actions: Name: your app name (users see it on the consent screen)
Kind: Web for a server-side OAuth client, Native for a mobile or desktop app
Environment: Sandbox
Redirect URI: your OAuth client's callback URL (http://localhost is allowed in Sandbox)
Scopes: pick the minimum set, for example users:read scheduled_events:read event_types:read, plus webhooks:write if you use webhooks
steps.agentNote: An agent can fill the form. Stop when the credentials page appears and hand over to a person.
steps.gotcha: New apps get no API access to anything outside the scopes you select. A scope you request in the authorize URL that is not enabled on the app returns 'requested scope is invalid, unknown or malformed'.

steps.title: Save the client ID, client secret and signing key
steps.detail: Calendly shows the Client ID, Client Secret and Webhook signing key once. Store them in your secret manager or enter them into your OAuth client's settings yourself.
actions: Copy Client ID
Copy Client Secret into secure storage
Copy Webhook signing key into secure storage
steps.agentNote: An agent can copy the Client ID. A person must handle the client secret and the signing key.
steps.gotcha: The secret and signing key are not shown again, even when you edit the app. If you lose them, you have to create a new app.

steps.title: Configure your OAuth client with Calendly endpoints
steps.detail: Authorize at https://auth.calendly.com/oauth/authorize and exchange the code at https://auth.calendly.com/oauth/token. Pass scopes space-separated and use PKCE with S256. Calendly recommends PKCE for all apps but does not enforce it for Web apps.
actions: Authorization URL: https://auth.calendly.com/oauth/authorize
Token URL: https://auth.calendly.com/oauth/token
Scopes: space-separated, exactly matching the scopes enabled on the app
Enable PKCE (S256)
steps.agentNote: An agent can set the non-secret fields. A person enters the client secret.
steps.gotcha: If your OAuth client sends PKCE parameters inconsistently, Calendly returns 'missing required parameter code_verifier'.

steps.title: Connect your own Calendly account
steps.detail: Run the authorize flow, approve the consent screen, and call GET https://api.calendly.com/users/me to confirm the token works.
steps.agentNote: An agent can run the test once a person has signed in to Calendly.

steps.title: Create a Production app with an HTTPS redirect
steps.detail: Create a second app with Environment = Production, your HTTPS redirect URI and the same scopes. Then save its new credentials and switch your OAuth client to them.
actions: Environment: Production
Redirect URI: your HTTPS callback URL
Scopes: same as the Sandbox app
A person saves the new client secret and signing key
steps.agentNote: An agent fills the form. A person handles the new secret.
steps.gotcha: A Production app rejects HTTP redirect URIs, including localhost.

scopes.intro: New OAuth apps get no API access until you select scopes. Calendly lists 23 scopes, and each :write scope includes the matching :read. The docs mention no scope that needs extra approval from Calendly. Apps created before scopes were introduced keep full access.

tiers.grants: Read the user's profile, booked meetings and event types
tiers.consequence: Nothing beyond user consent

tiers.grants: Create webhook subscriptions
tiers.consequence: No review, but it only works if the user has a Standard, Teams or Enterprise plan

tiers.grants: Org admin, data deletion and audit log access
tiers.consequence: No review is documented. Some of these endpoints are Enterprise-only or need an org admin

blockers.symptom: 'An error has occurred: the requested scope is invalid, unknown or malformed'
blockers.cause: The authorize URL asks for scope names that are not enabled on the app, or that are formatted wrongly (commas, dot-style names, stray characters).
blockers.fix: Use exactly the scope names enabled on the app, separated by spaces.

blockers.symptom: Webhook subscription creation fails for some users
blockers.cause: Webhooks need the user to be on a Standard, Teams or Enterprise plan.
blockers.fix: Check the user's plan, or fall back to polling the API for users on Free.

blockers.symptom: Connected users suddenly get 401 errors
blockers.cause: Calendly revokes tokens when the user changes their login email, password or login method.
blockers.fix: Handle 401 errors by asking the user to reconnect.

unknowns.question: Does anyone at Calendly approve the scopes on a new app, or do they only need user consent?
unknowns.why: The scopes page says access needs scopes 'requested and approved' but does not name the approver. No source describes a Calendly review.
unknowns.resolve: Create a Production app with your scopes and check that a different Calendly account can connect right away.

unknowns.question: Are there connection caps, or other differences between Sandbox and Production apps besides redirect URI rules?
unknowns.why: The docs only describe the redirect URI difference.
unknowns.resolve: Check the developer console or ask in the Calendly community's API & Webhook Help forum.

agentCan: Fill the app creation form in the developer console
Copy the Client ID and redirect URI
Set the authorize and token URLs, scopes and PKCE in your OAuth client
Run a test connection once a person has signed in
youMust: Sign up for the developer account with GitHub or Google
Save the client secret and webhook signing key, and enter them into your OAuth client
Confirm users have a paid plan if you rely on webhooks

name: Linear
summary: Linear is self-serve. You create an OAuth app in your workspace settings, turn on the Public switch, and any Linear workspace can install it right away, with no app review. The only review is the optional listing in Linear's integration directory, which accepts only integrations built by formal companies.
tierReason: Once the Public switch is on, other workspaces can authorize the app straight away, and Linear's docs describe no review, verification or user cap before that.

composio.note: Composio has a managed Linear OAuth app, so you can prototype before you register your own. Register your own before launch so your app name shows on the consent screen. Composio's separate LINEAR_MCP toolkit needs your own OAuth app.

stages.name: Your workspace
stages.whoCanConnect: Members of the workspace that owns the app (apps are private by default)
stages.userSees: Linear's authorization screen with your app name and the requested scopes
stages.unlock: Turn on the Public switch (distribution: public) on the OAuth app

stages.name: Public app
stages.whoCanConnect: Any Linear workspace. On Enterprise workspaces with app approvals turned on, an admin may have to approve the app first.
stages.userSees: The same authorization screen. Members of workspaces that require approval see a request screen until an admin approves the app.

requirements.label: A Linear workspace where you are an admin
requirements.detail: Linear recommends a dedicated workspace just for managing the OAuth app, because every admin of that workspace can access the app and its credentials.

requirements.label: Your redirect URI
requirements.detail: Your OAuth client's callback URL. It must be an absolute HTTP or HTTPS URL, and an app can register up to 32 of them.

requirements.label: A homepage or docs URL and a developer name
requirements.detail: The app record requires a homepage or documentation URL, a developer name, and an app name that does not contain the word "Linear".

requirements.label: Directory assets (optional)
requirements.detail: You only need these to be listed in Linear's integration directory: a 320×320 color icon, a 320×320 white monochrome icon, and 1–3 showcase images at 1600×1000. Linear only lists integrations built by formal companies.

steps.title: Open OAuth applications in workspace settings
steps.detail: Sign in to Linear as a workspace admin. Go to Settings > API > OAuth applications and click + to create an app.
actions: Sign in at linear.app
Go to Settings > API > OAuth applications
Click + (or open linear.app/settings/api/applications/new)
steps.agentNote: Once you are signed in, an agent can open the page and fill in the form.
steps.gotcha: If you create the app in your personal workspace, only that workspace's admins can manage it. Use a dedicated workspace instead.

steps.title: Fill in the app details and callback URLs
steps.detail: Enter the app name, developer name, homepage URL, an optional description and icon, and your redirect URI under Callback URLs. Leave Refresh Tokens turned on (the default for new apps).
actions: Application name (must not contain "Linear")
Developer name
Developer/homepage URL
Callback URLs: your redirect URI
Confirm Refresh Tokens is enabled
Optionally turn on webhooks and pick resource types
steps.agentNote: An agent can fill in every field. Stop before the secrets are shown.
steps.gotcha: The redirect_uri in your authorize request must exactly match a registered callback URL. A mismatch causes an 'Invalid redirect URI' error.

steps.title: Turn on the Public switch
steps.detail: Apps are private by default and can only be installed in the workspace that created them. Turn on Public so other workspaces can install the app. Linear documents no review for this.
actions: Turn on Public
Click Create
steps.agentNote: An agent can flip the switch, but you should confirm you want other workspaces to be able to install the app.
steps.gotcha: If you leave it private, users from other workspaces can't authorize the app.

steps.title: Store the client ID and secret
steps.detail: Copy the client ID and client secret (plus the webhook signing secret, if you use webhooks) into your OAuth client's secret storage. You can rotate each secret separately later.
actions: Copy Client ID
Copy Client Secret into your secret store
Copy the webhook signing secret if you need it
steps.agentNote: An agent can copy the client ID. You handle the client secret.
steps.gotcha: Rotating the client secret invalidates client_credentials tokens but does not revoke existing user tokens.

steps.title: Configure your OAuth client and scopes
steps.detail: Use authorize URL https://linear.app/oauth/authorize and token URL https://api.linear.app/oauth/token. Request scopes separated by commas (read, write, issues:create, comments:create, admin), and optionally actor=app. Access tokens last 24 hours, and each refresh returns a new refresh token.
actions: Set the authorize and token URLs
Set scopes, e.g. read,write
Store the rotated refresh token after every refresh
Test by connecting your own workspace
steps.agentNote: An agent can set everything except the secret, which you enter yourself.
steps.gotcha: Refresh tokens rotate, so reusing an old one returns invalid_grant. Save the new refresh token from every refresh response.

steps.title: Optionally apply for the integration directory
steps.detail: You don't need a listing for users to connect. To be listed, submit Linear's form and send your assets to integrations@linear.app. Linear says it generally rejects scripts, hobby projects and low-effort apps.
actions: Complete the submission form
Email assets to integrations@linear.app
steps.agentNote: An agent can draft the copy. You submit the form and the assets.

scopes.intro: Linear doesn't classify scopes or require approval for any of them. Request the narrowest set that works. The admin scope is the broadest one.

tiers.grants: Read access (always included)
tiers.consequence: Nothing

tiers.grants: Write access, or narrower create-only access
tiers.consequence: Nothing

tiers.grants: Admin-level endpoints
tiers.consequence: No review. Linear advises requesting it only when absolutely needed. Installing users likely need to be admins (not confirmed).

blockers.symptom: Users from other workspaces can't install the app
blockers.cause: The app is still private, which is the default distribution.
blockers.fix: Turn on Public in the app settings.

blockers.symptom: 'Invalid redirect URI' at authorization
blockers.cause: The redirect_uri sent doesn't match any registered callback URL.
blockers.fix: Add the exact URL under Callback URLs.

blockers.symptom: invalid_grant on refresh
blockers.cause: A stale refresh token was reused after rotation.
blockers.fix: Save the new refresh token after each refresh. Linear allows replaying the original request within 30 minutes if a response is lost.

blockers.symptom: A member sees an approval request screen instead of consent
blockers.cause: Their Enterprise workspace has third-party app approvals turned on.
blockers.fix: A workspace admin approves the app under workspace applications.

unknowns.question: Does making an app Public ever trigger a review by Linear?
unknowns.why: The docs describe the switch but say nothing about review.
unknowns.resolve: Create a test app, turn on Public, and install it from a second workspace.

unknowns.question: Do actor=app installs or the admin scope require a workspace admin to authorize?
unknowns.why: Not confirmed in the pages fetched.
unknowns.resolve: Check the Linear app/agent authentication docs, or test with a non-admin account.

unknowns.question: How long does a directory listing review take?
unknowns.why: Linear gives no timeline.
unknowns.resolve: Ask integrations@linear.app.

agentCan: Open the OAuth app form and fill in the name, URLs and callback URLs
Configure your OAuth client's endpoints, scopes and client ID
Test a connection with your own workspace
youMust: Sign in as a workspace admin (ideally in a dedicated workspace)
Turn on Public and click Create
Copy and store the client secret
Optionally submit the directory listing

name: Slack
summary: Any workspace can install your Slack app over OAuth on the same day: you create the app, complete the distribution checklist and turn on public distribution, with no review. The catch is that unlisted apps get severe rate limits on reading message history (conversations.history and conversations.replies drop to 1 request per minute). Lifting that limit means getting into the Slack Marketplace, which requires 10+ active installs and a review that can take up to about 12 weeks.
tierReason: Public OAuth distribution needs no review, but unlisted (non-Marketplace) apps are limited to 1 request per minute and 15 objects per call on conversations.history and conversations.replies until they pass Marketplace review.

composio.note: Composio has a managed Slack OAuth app, so you can prototype before you register your own. Register your own app before launch so your name appears on the install screen. A shared app is also unlikely to give you Marketplace-level rate limits.

stages.name: Your workspace
stages.whoCanConnect: Only the workspace that owns the app (its development workspace).
stages.userSees: The standard Slack install/consent screen listing the requested bot and user scopes.
stages.unlock: Complete the Manage Distribution checklist and click Activate Public Distribution.

stages.name: Unlisted public distribution
stages.whoCanConnect: Any Slack workspace, through your install URL or Add to Slack button. Admins in some workspaces must approve the app first.
stages.userSees: The standard consent screen. There is no Marketplace listing, and the workspace may show an admin-approval request.
stages.unlock: Reach 10+ active workspace installs, then pass Slack Marketplace review. You only need this if you want the higher rate limits or a listing.

stages.name: Slack Marketplace
stages.whoCanConnect: Any workspace. Users can also install directly from the Marketplace, and the normal rate limits apply.
stages.userSees: A Marketplace listing page plus the standard consent screen.

requirements.label: A Slack workspace you can sign in to
requirements.detail: Apps are created under a Slack account and owned by a development workspace.

requirements.label: An HTTPS redirect URI
requirements.detail: Redirect URLs must use HTTPS and can't contain '#'. Event and interaction URLs also need SSL.

requirements.label: A working OAuth v2 flow
requirements.detail: Distributed apps must use OAuth to get a token for each workspace and user. A single-workspace install doesn't need it.

requirements.label: 10+ active workspace installs
requirements.detail: Marketplace submission requires installs on at least 10 workspaces active in the past 28 days, and that count must hold for the whole review.

requirements.label: Demo video and reviewer test account
requirements.detail: You need a video showing install, OAuth, setup, use and uninstall. You also need test credentials with dummy data for your service.

steps.title: Create a Slack app
steps.detail: Sign in at api.slack.com/apps and create a new app, either from scratch or from a manifest. Pick the development workspace that will own it.
actions: Click Create New App
Choose From scratch or From an app manifest
Enter an app name and select the development workspace
steps.agentNote: Once you're signed in, an agent can fill the form or paste a manifest.
steps.gotcha: The development workspace owns the app. Pick one you'll keep long-term.

steps.title: Add your redirect URI and scopes
steps.detail: Under OAuth & Permissions, add your redirect URI (HTTPS) and the bot scopes and user scopes your integration needs. Request only what you use, because workspace admins may have to approve the app.
actions: Open OAuth & Permissions
Add your redirect URI under Redirect URLs and save
Add Bot Token Scopes and/or User Token Scopes
steps.agentNote: An agent can do all of this. It should not copy the client secret.
steps.gotcha: If you configure several redirect URLs, send the same redirect_uri in the authorize call and in oauth.v2.access, or you'll get bad_redirect_uri.

steps.title: Put the client ID and secret into your OAuth client
steps.detail: Copy the Client ID and Client Secret from Basic Information > App Credentials into your OAuth client. Set the authorize URL to https://slack.com/oauth/v2/authorize and the token URL to https://slack.com/api/oauth.v2.access.
actions: Copy the Client ID
Copy the Client Secret into your secret store
Use the scope parameter for bot scopes and user_scope for user scopes
steps.agentNote: An agent can enter the client ID and the URLs. A person handles the client secret.
steps.gotcha: User tokens come back under authed_user, not at the top level of the token response.

steps.title: Test an install on your own workspace
steps.detail: Run the OAuth flow against your development workspace and confirm that a token comes back.
steps.agentNote: An agent can run the flow. A person may need to click Allow.
steps.gotcha: Installing in any other workspace before you enable distribution fails with invalid_team_for_non_distributed_app.

steps.title: Activate public distribution
steps.detail: In Manage Distribution, complete every checklist item (for example, remove hard-coded tokens and use HTTPS), then click Activate Public Distribution. No review is involved. You get a shareable install URL and an Add to Slack button.
actions: Open Manage Distribution
Complete each checklist item
Click Activate Public Distribution
steps.agentNote: An agent can work through the checklist. A person should confirm activation.
steps.gotcha: Unlisted apps created after May 29, 2025 get conversations.history and conversations.replies at 1 request per minute and 15 objects per call. Plan around this if you read message history.

steps.title: Get 10+ active workspace installs
steps.detail: Marketplace submission requires at least 10 installs on workspaces active in the past 28 days. Test install, use and uninstall on a workspace other than your development one.
steps.gotcha: If installs drop below 10 during review, the submission is affected.

steps.title: Submit to the Slack Marketplace
steps.detail: Fill in the listing, write a justification for each scope, provide reviewer test credentials, and record a demo video covering install, OAuth, setup, use and uninstall. Fix anything the automated tests flag before you submit.
actions: Fill in the listing info and support details
Justify every requested scope
Provide test account credentials with dummy data
Upload the demo video
Run the automated tests and submit
steps.agentNote: An agent can draft listing copy and scope justifications. A person records the video and submits.
steps.gotcha: Legacy, restricted and broad data-access scopes aren't allowed. Failing preliminary review resets your place in the queue.

steps.title: Wait for preliminary and functional review
steps.detail: Preliminary review takes up to 10 business days. Functional review takes up to 10 weeks for new apps. Once approved, you choose when to publish.
steps.gotcha: Reviews can't be expedited, so plan for several rounds of feedback.

scopes.intro: Slack doesn't classify scopes for OAuth approval. Any scope works for unlisted distribution. Marketplace review checks each scope and rejects some.

tiers.grants: Normal app functions
tiers.consequence: Nothing for unlisted apps. A scope justification during Marketplace review.

tiers.grants: Reading message history
tiers.consequence: Allowed, but unlisted apps are limited to 1 request per minute and 15 objects per call until Marketplace approval.

tiers.scope: Legacy, restricted or broad data-access scopes
tiers.grants: Wide workspace data access
tiers.consequence: Not allowed in the Marketplace.

blockers.symptom: invalid_team_for_non_distributed_app when another workspace installs
blockers.cause: Public distribution hasn't been activated.
blockers.fix: Complete the Manage Distribution checklist and activate public distribution.

blockers.symptom: bad_redirect_uri during token exchange
blockers.cause: The redirect_uri differs between the authorize call and oauth.v2.access, or doesn't match a configured Redirect URL.
blockers.fix: Send the same redirect_uri in both calls, and make sure it matches (or is a subdirectory of) a configured URL.

blockers.symptom: ratelimited errors and 15-message pages on conversations.history/replies
blockers.cause: Unlisted commercial apps are limited to Tier 1 (1 request per minute) for these methods.
blockers.fix: Get listed in the Slack Marketplace, or design around the limit (for example, use the Events API to capture messages as they arrive).

blockers.symptom: unapproved_scope error
blockers.cause: A published app requested a scope that Slack hasn't approved for it.
blockers.fix: Request only approved scopes, or submit the new scopes for Marketplace review.

unknowns.question: Do the reduced rate limits now apply to existing installs of unlisted apps?
unknowns.why: Slack's own pages conflict. Dates given include Sept 2, 2025 and March 3, 2026, and one page says existing installs are exempt.
unknowns.resolve: Check the current rate-limits page and the 2025-05 terms FAQ on docs.slack.dev, or test against an existing install.

unknowns.question: How long Marketplace reviews actually take in practice
unknowns.why: I found only Slack's stated maximums, no developer reports.
unknowns.resolve: Check the estimated time shown on your app's submission page.

Enter the client ID and the authorize/token URLs into your OAuth client
Work through the distribution checklist
Run test installs

Handle the client secret
Click Activate Public Distribution

name: Salesforce
summary: You can connect your own org through an External Client App (ECA) in under an hour. Letting any customer's org connect is harder. Since Spring '26 you can't create new Connected Apps by default, so you have to ship your ECA in a second-generation (2GP) managed package. Each customer org then installs that package, or its admin approves your app. Salesforce doesn't review the app unless you want an AppExchange listing.
tierReason: No Salesforce review is needed before other orgs can connect, but you must package and distribute the ECA yourself, and each customer org's admin controls whether it can be used. The AppExchange security review applies only if you want a public listing.

composio.note: Composio has a managed Salesforce OAuth app, so you can prototype before building your own ECA. Customer orgs may still need their admin to approve or install that app, and your name won't be on the consent screen until you use your own.

totals.firstConnection: Today, in about 30–60 minutes, using a free Developer Edition org and a Local ECA

stages.name: Your org
stages.whoCanConnect: Users of the org where you created a Local External Client App
stages.userSees: The standard Salesforce login, then an 'Allow Access' consent screen showing your app name and scopes
stages.unlock: Create a Packaged ECA, put it in a 2GP managed package and promote a released version

stages.name: Customer orgs
stages.whoCanConnect: Users in any Salesforce org that has installed your managed package and whose policies let users self-authorize
stages.userSees: The Salesforce login and consent screen. Before that, an admin installs your package from its install URL, or from AppExchange if you're listed.

requirements.label: Salesforce org with ECA permission
requirements.detail: ECAs are available in Professional, Performance, Unlimited and Developer editions. A free Developer Edition org works. Your user needs the 'Create, Edit, and Delete External Client Apps' permission.

requirements.label: Redirect URI
requirements.detail: The callback URL of your OAuth client, which you enter on the ECA.

requirements.label: Dev Hub org and namespace org
requirements.detail: Packaging needs a Dev Hub plus a separate org that registers a namespace. One org can't do both. The Dev Hub must stay alive for as long as the package is used, because it holds the global OAuth settings.

requirements.label: Salesforce CLI
requirements.detail: You use the Salesforce CLI to create the 2GP package and its package versions.

requirements.label: Customer admin cooperation
requirements.detail: Each customer org's admin has to install your package. Otherwise users need the 'Approve Uninstalled Connected Apps' or 'Use Any API Client' permission before they can authorize an app that isn't installed.

steps.title: Sign up for a Developer Edition org
steps.detail: Create a free Developer Edition org, or use an org you already have in a supported edition. Make sure your user can create External Client Apps.
steps.agentNote: A person has to sign up and verify the email address.
steps.gotcha: Nango's guide reports invalid_client_id errors when the developer user's password contains special characters.

steps.title: Create an External Client App
steps.detail: In Setup, open External Client App Manager and create a new app. Choose Local for single-org testing, or Packaged if you will distribute it. Enable OAuth and enter your redirect URI.
actions: Setup > Quick Find 'External Client App Manager' > New External Client App
Fill in the app name, API name and contact email
Distribution State: Local (testing) or Packaged (multi-org)
Enable OAuth; Callback URL = your redirect URI
Scopes: 'Manage user data via APIs (api)' and 'Perform requests at any time (refresh_token, offline_access)'
Enable the Authorization Code and Credentials flow; leave 'Require secret' and 'Require PKCE' on
Policies tab: Refresh Token Policy = valid until revoked
steps.agentNote: An agent can fill in this form once a person is signed in. A person should copy the consumer secret.
steps.gotcha: New Connected Apps are disabled by default since Spring '26. Don't follow older guides that tell you to create one in App Manager.

steps.title: Copy consumer key and secret into your client
steps.detail: Open the app's Settings tab, reveal the Consumer Key and Consumer Secret, and store them in your OAuth client. Use https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/authorize and /token, or test.salesforce.com for sandboxes.
steps.agentNote: An agent can set the key and endpoints. A person handles the secret.
steps.gotcha: Every customer org has its own instance_url, which comes back in the token response. Store it for each connection.

steps.title: Test a connection with your own org
steps.detail: Run the authorization code flow, approve access, and call an API endpoint using the returned instance_url.
steps.agentNote: An agent can run the test. A person signs in.
steps.gotcha: Changes to ECA settings may take a few minutes to apply.

steps.title: Set up a Dev Hub and register a namespace
steps.detail: Enable Dev Hub in one org, register a namespace in a separate org, and link the namespace to the Dev Hub in Namespace Registries.
steps.agentNote: An agent can click through Setup once a person is signed in to both orgs.
steps.gotcha: You can't enable Dev Hub and register a namespace in the same org.

steps.title: Package the Packaged ECA in a 2GP package
steps.detail: Create the ECA in the Dev Hub with Distribution State set to Packaged. Then use the CLI to create a managed package, retrieve the ECA metadata, create a package version and promote it to released. Leave the global OAuth settings out of the package and keep them in the Dev Hub.
actions: sf org login web (Dev Hub)
sf package create --package-type Managed
Retrieve the ECA metadata; set the namespace and package ID in sfdx-project.json
sf package version create, then sf package version promote
steps.agentNote: An agent can run the CLI commands once a person has authenticated the CLI.
steps.gotcha: One community report says a packaged ECA failed in subscriber orgs with OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_BLOCKED 'Cross-org OAuth flows are not supported'. Check how the OAuth link is configured in an installed test org before you launch.

steps.title: Give customers the package install URL
steps.detail: Send customers' admins the install URL and ask them to set the app's policy so users can self-authorize. Install it in a second test org first to confirm that OAuth works across orgs.
steps.agentNote: An agent can test in a second org once a person is signed in.
steps.gotcha: Users in orgs that haven't installed the app are blocked unless they hold the Approve Uninstalled Connected Apps or Use Any API Client permission.

steps.title: Optionally submit for AppExchange security review
steps.detail: You need this only for a public AppExchange listing. Older Salesforce docs list a $2,550 review fee plus a $150 listing fee for paid solutions, and no fee for free ones.
steps.agentNote: Joining the partner program, paying and submitting have to be done by a person.
steps.gotcha: The fees above come from older doc versions, so check the current Packaging Guide.

blockers.symptom: You can't create a Connected App, or the option is missing in App Manager
blockers.cause: Since Spring '26, creating new Connected Apps is disabled by default in every org, both in the UI and through the API
blockers.fix: Use an External Client App. Salesforce Support can grant a temporary exception, but Salesforce has said it will remove that option.

blockers.symptom: Users in a customer org get blocked at authorization because the app isn't installed
blockers.cause: Since September 2025, users need the Approve Uninstalled Connected Apps or Use Any API Client permission to authorize apps that aren't installed
blockers.fix: Have the customer admin install your package or app, or grant that permission to the users who connect

blockers.symptom: OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_BLOCKED: Cross-org OAuth flows are not supported for this external client app
blockers.cause: Unclear. One community reply points to how the global OAuth settings and the OAuth link are set up on the packaged ECA.
blockers.fix: Make sure the subscriber ECA refers to the source org's global OAuth settings, and keep the source org alive. If it still fails, contact Salesforce support.

unknowns.question: Does a packaged ECA support cross-org web-server OAuth with one consumer key out of the box?
unknowns.why: The only community thread on this has no confirmed fix, and the official docs returned 403 to the fetcher
unknowns.resolve: Install your package in a second Developer Edition org and test, or read help.salesforce.com 'External Client Apps' packaging docs

unknowns.question: Do the uninstalled-app permission rules apply to ECAs the same way they apply to Connected Apps?
unknowns.why: The sources only discuss Connected Apps
unknowns.resolve: Test with an org that hasn't installed your package, and check Salesforce help

unknowns.question: What are the current AppExchange security review fees and turnaround times?
unknowns.why: Only older doc versions were found, with no timeline
unknowns.resolve: Check the latest ISVforce/Packaging Guide or ask your Partner Account Manager

agentCan: Fill in the ECA form and OAuth settings
Configure your OAuth client with the consumer key and endpoints
Run CLI packaging commands after a person authenticates
Test connections in your own org and in test orgs
youMust: Sign up for and sign in to the Salesforce orgs
Copy and store the consumer secret
Register a namespace and enable Dev Hub
Get customer admins to install the package
Pay for and submit the AppExchange security review if you want a listing

sources.title: Salesforce connected apps and external client apps
Package and distribute external client apps
Cross-org OAuth blocked for packaged ECA
New Connected Apps Can No Longer Be Created in Spring '26
How the AppExchange Security Review Submission Loop Works

name: Gmail
summary: You can connect your own account and up to 100 test users the same day. The scopes most Gmail integrations need (gmail.readonly, gmail.modify, gmail.compose) are restricted, so a public launch needs Google's OAuth verification and a paid, annual third-party CASA security assessment. Expect several weeks.
tierReason: Typical Gmail scopes are restricted, and Google requires a paid third-party CASA security assessment (assessor fees of about $500–$4,500, renewed every year) before the public can connect.

composio.note: Composio has a managed Gmail OAuth app, so you can prototype without registering your own. To have your own name on the consent screen, you have to register your own app and go through Google's verification and CASA yourself.

totals.firstConnection: Today, in about 30–60 minutes, with your own account added as a test user

stages.name: Your account
stages.whoCanConnect: You, added as a test user on an External app in Testing status, or anyone in your Workspace org if the app is Internal.
stages.userSees: A Google 'hasn't verified this app' warning before consent. Grants expire after 7 days.
stages.unlock: Add other Google accounts to the test-user list.

stages.name: Test users
stages.whoCanConnect: Up to 100 test users you list by email. Each one counts against a quota that does not reset.
stages.userSees: An unverified-app warning. Grants and refresh tokens expire 7 days after consent, so users have to reconnect weekly.
stages.unlock: Publish to production, submit for verification, pass restricted-scope review and the CASA security assessment.

stages.name: Public launch
stages.whoCanConnect: Any Google account.
stages.userSees: A normal consent screen with your app name and logo, listing the Gmail permissions requested.

requirements.label: Google account and Google Cloud project
requirements.detail: Any Google account can create a Cloud project. Internal apps need a Google Cloud Organization, which comes from Workspace or Cloud Identity.

requirements.label: Verified domain you own
requirements.detail: Your homepage, privacy policy and redirect domains must be authorized domains, verified in Google Search Console.

requirements.label: Public homepage and privacy policy
requirements.detail: The homepage must be public, not behind a login. The privacy policy must include the Google API Services Limited Use disclosure and explain how Gmail data is handled.

requirements.label: Demo video
requirements.detail: An English video showing the full OAuth flow, the consent screen with the exact scopes requested, and each feature that uses each scope.

requirements.label: CASA security assessment (paid, annual)
requirements.detail: Required if you store or transmit restricted-scope data on servers. A Google-empanelled assessor does it. You pay the assessor about $500–$4,500, and the Letter of Validation must be renewed every 12 months.

steps.title: Create a Google Cloud project
steps.detail: Sign in to the Google Cloud console and create a project for the app. Google recommends separate projects for development and production.
actions: Sign in at console.cloud.google.com
Create a new project and name it
steps.agentNote: Once you're signed in, an agent can create the project.
steps.gotcha: The 100-user unverified cap applies for the project's lifetime and never resets, so keep test traffic in a separate dev project.

steps.title: Enable the Gmail API
steps.detail: In the API Library, find the Gmail API and enable it for the project.
actions: APIs & Services > Library > Gmail API > Enable
steps.agentNote: An agent can do this in the console.

steps.title: Configure the OAuth consent screen
steps.detail: In Google Auth Platform, set the user type to External (or Internal for your org only) and fill in branding: app name, support email, logo, homepage, privacy policy, terms, authorized domains and developer contact.
actions: Choose user type: External or Internal
Fill in app name, user support email and developer contact email
Add homepage, privacy policy and terms URLs
Add authorized domains
steps.agentNote: An agent can fill in the form. You choose the support and contact emails.
steps.gotcha: Use a contact inbox someone monitors. Google sends all verification messages there.

steps.title: Add the narrowest Gmail scopes you need
steps.detail: On the Data Access page, add only the scopes your live features use. gmail.send is sensitive. gmail.readonly, gmail.modify, gmail.compose, gmail.metadata and https://mail.google.com/ are restricted.
actions: Data Access > Add or remove scopes
Pick the narrowest scope that works, for example gmail.send for send-only apps
steps.agentNote: An agent can add the scopes once you've decided which ones you need.
steps.gotcha: Scopes on the consent screen must match what your app actually requests. A mismatch is a common reason for rejection.

steps.title: Create a Web application OAuth client
steps.detail: Create an OAuth client ID of type Web application and add your redirect URI under Authorized redirect URIs. A person should copy the client secret into your OAuth client's configuration.
actions: Clients > Create client > Web application
Add your redirect URI exactly as your OAuth client sends it
You copy the client ID and secret into your OAuth client
steps.agentNote: An agent can create the client and enter your redirect URI. It hands off to you before the secret is shown.
steps.gotcha: Request access_type=offline and prompt=consent so you get a refresh token.

steps.title: Add test users and connect
steps.detail: While the app is in Testing status, add your account and up to 99 others under Audience > Test users, then run a test connection through your OAuth client.
actions: Audience > Test users > Add users
Connect your own account through your OAuth client and call the Gmail API
steps.agentNote: An agent can add the emails and run a test connection. You sign in to Google during consent.
steps.gotcha: In Testing, grants and refresh tokens expire after 7 days, and each test user permanently uses up one of the 100 slots.

steps.title: Verify domain ownership in Search Console
steps.detail: Verify the domains for your homepage, privacy policy and redirect URIs in Google Search Console, using an account that is an owner or editor on the project.
actions: Add a DNS TXT record or use another Search Console verification method
steps.agentNote: An agent can start the Search Console flow. You make the DNS change.
steps.gotcha: An unverified callback or homepage domain is a common rejection reason.

steps.title: Record demo video and write justifications
steps.detail: Record an English demo showing the consent screen with the exact scopes and every feature that uses each scope. For each scope, write which feature uses it and why a narrower scope won't work.
actions: Upload the video as unlisted on YouTube
Draft a justification for each scope
Add the Limited Use disclosure to your privacy policy
steps.agentNote: An agent can draft justifications. You record the video.
steps.gotcha: Vague justifications and videos that don't show the real consent screen are the most common reasons for resubmission.

steps.title: Publish the app and submit for verification
steps.detail: Click Publish app to move to production, then use Prepare for verification in the Verification Center, add the justifications and video link, and submit.
actions: Audience > Publish app
Verification Center > Prepare for verification > Submit
steps.agentNote: An agent can fill in the forms. You submit.
steps.gotcha: If you change anything after submitting, you have to resubmit the form or review stalls.

steps.title: Wait for Trust & Safety review
steps.detail: Google's OAuth review team emails project owners and editors, often within 24–48 hours, and may ask for changes. Approval of the use case often comes in under a week, and Google's own estimate is several weeks.
steps.gotcha: Reply within a day. Each back-and-forth adds days.

steps.title: Complete the CASA security assessment
steps.detail: When Google tells you to start, hire an empanelled CASA assessor (most apps are Tier 2), fix any scan findings and get a Letter of Validation. Assessor fees run about $500–$4,500.
actions: Choose an assessor from the App Defense Alliance list
Run SAST/DAST scans and answer the questionnaire
Fix findings and get the Letter of Validation
steps.agentNote: An agent can help prepare the questionnaire answers. You pay and deal with the assessor.
steps.gotcha: Pick an assessor early. Tier 3 (for example, with domain-wide delegation) costs much more.

steps.title: Wait for CASA and final approval
steps.detail: Google says Tier 2 assessments take 2–3 weeks. After the Letter of Validation, Google may take up to a week to grant final approval.
steps.gotcha: Restricted-scope verification and CASA must be renewed every 12 months. Start 60–90 days before expiry.

scopes.intro: Google classifies Gmail scopes into three levels. The level decides what review you go through. Most read or modify integrations need restricted scopes.

tiers.grants: View and edit labels
tiers.consequence: Brand verification only, if you want your name and logo shown

tiers.grants: Send email as the user
tiers.consequence: OAuth app verification (demo video, justification). No CASA.

tiers.grants: Read messages and settings, or headers and labels only
tiers.consequence: Restricted-scope verification plus annual CASA assessment if data reaches your servers

tiers.grants: Read, write, send, drafts and settings
tiers.consequence: Restricted-scope verification plus annual CASA assessment

tiers.grants: Full mailbox access, including permanent delete
tiers.consequence: Restricted review. Google asks you to request it only if you need permanent deletion.

blockers.symptom: Users see 'Google hasn't verified this app' and new sign-ups stop after 100 users
blockers.cause: The app is unverified and uses sensitive or restricted scopes. The 100-user cap applies for the project's lifetime and cannot be reset.
blockers.fix: Complete verification. Keep development in a separate project so you don't use up the production quota.

blockers.symptom: invalid_grant on refresh after about a week
blockers.cause: In Testing status, grants and refresh tokens expire 7 days after consent.
blockers.fix: Have users reconnect, or publish to production and get verified.

blockers.symptom: Error 403: org_internal
blockers.cause: The app's user type is Internal, and the user is outside your Google Cloud organization.
blockers.fix: Switch the user type to External.

blockers.symptom: Verification sent back for resubmission
blockers.cause: Common causes: scope mismatch, unused scopes, weak demo video, vague justifications, homepage behind a login, missing Limited Use disclosure.
blockers.fix: Fix every listed issue, re-record the video if needed and resubmit the form.

unknowns.question: Exact end-to-end time for Gmail restricted-scope approval
unknowns.why: Google gives no Gmail-specific timeline. The CASA figures come from a Google Health API page, and the rest from vendor reports.
unknowns.resolve: Watch the Verification Center and the emails Google sends to your contact address after you submit.

unknowns.question: Which CASA tier and fee your app will get
unknowns.why: Google assigns the tier based on user count, scopes and other risk signals.
unknowns.resolve: Google Trust & Safety tells you the tier when the assessment starts. Ask assessors for quotes.

unknowns.question: Whether you can skip CASA by keeping all Gmail data on the client
unknowns.why: The docs say the assessment applies when restricted data is stored or transmitted on servers, but Google decides each case during review.
unknowns.resolve: Describe your data flow in the submission and confirm with the review team.

agentCan: Enable the Gmail API
Fill in the consent screen branding and Data Access scopes
Create the Web OAuth client and enter your redirect URI
Add test users and run a test connection
Draft scope justifications and CASA questionnaire answers
youMust: Sign in and create the Google Cloud project
Copy the client secret into your OAuth client
Verify domains in Search Console
Record the demo video
Submit for verification and answer Google's emails
Pay for and complete the CASA assessment every year

name: Spotify
summary: You can register an app and connect your own account in minutes. To go further you need a Premium subscription, and reaching the public requires extended quota, which Spotify grants only to registered businesses with at least 250k monthly active users after a review of up to six weeks.
tierReason: Development mode caps you at 5 allowlisted users, and since May 15, 2025 only registered organizations with at least 250k MAU and a launched service can apply for extended quota.

composio.note: Composio has no managed Spotify app, so you register your own Spotify app and enter its client ID and secret in Composio. Because the developer pays for it, your Spotify account needs Premium.

totals.firstConnection: Today, in about 15 minutes, if your Spotify account has Premium

stages.name: Your account
stages.whoCanConnect: You, the app owner. Your account must have an active Premium subscription.
stages.userSees: Spotify's consent screen with your app name and description.
stages.unlock: Add up to 5 users to the app's allowlist under Users and Access.

stages.name: Development mode
stages.whoCanConnect: Up to 5 Spotify users you add to the allowlist by name and email. Anyone else gets 403 errors.
stages.userSees: The normal consent screen. Some endpoints and response fields aren't available in development mode.
stages.unlock: Get approved through the Partner Application, then get your quota extension request approved. You must be a registered organization with at least 250k MAU.

stages.name: Extended quota
stages.whoCanConnect: Any Spotify user. The allowlist no longer applies.
stages.userSees: The normal consent screen.

requirements.label: Spotify Premium on the owner account
requirements.detail: Development-mode apps stop working if the owner's Premium subscription lapses. They start working again when the owner resubscribes.

requirements.label: HTTPS redirect URI or loopback IP
requirements.detail: Redirect URIs must use HTTPS. For local testing you can use http://127.0.0.1 or http://[::1]. The hostname 'localhost' is rejected.

requirements.label: Legally registered business or organization
requirements.detail: Spotify hasn't accepted extended quota requests from individuals since May 15, 2025.

requirements.label: Launched service with at least 250k MAU
requirements.detail: You need an active, launched service with at least 250k monthly active users. It must be available in key Spotify markets, be commercially viable and comply with Spotify's terms.

requirements.label: Company email address
requirements.detail: You must submit the Partner Application from a company email address.

steps.title: Sign in to the Spotify Developer Dashboard
steps.detail: Sign in with the Spotify account that will own the app. This account needs active Premium.
actions: Open developer.spotify.com/dashboard
Sign in and accept the developer terms if prompted
steps.gotcha: If the owner account is on the free plan, development-mode apps don't work.

steps.title: Create the app
steps.detail: Click Create app and fill in the name and description. Users see both on the consent screen. Add a website and your redirect URI, select Web API, and accept the Developer Terms. A person should confirm the terms checkbox.
actions: App name and App description
Website (optional)
Redirect URIs: your OAuth client's callback URL, which must match exactly
Select the Web API
Check the Developer Terms of Service box and click Save
steps.agentNote: An agent can fill in the form. A person should accept the Developer Terms.
steps.gotcha: 'localhost' redirect URIs are rejected. Use 127.0.0.1 or an HTTPS URL.

steps.title: Copy the client ID and secret into your OAuth client
steps.detail: Under Settings, copy the client ID and reveal the client secret. Store both in your OAuth client. The authorize URL is https://accounts.spotify.com/authorize and the token URL is https://accounts.spotify.com/api/token.
actions: Open the app, then Settings
Copy the Client ID
Click View client secret and store it securely
steps.agentNote: An agent can copy the client ID. A person handles the client secret.
steps.gotcha: If the secret leaks, rotate it. Rotating breaks existing configurations until you update them.

steps.title: Connect your own Spotify account
steps.detail: Run the authorization flow with the scopes you need, for example user-read-email or playlist-read-private, and confirm API calls succeed.
actions: Start the OAuth flow from your OAuth client
Approve the consent screen
Call /v1/me to verify the token
steps.agentNote: An agent can drive the test. A person may need to sign in to Spotify.
steps.gotcha: Development-mode apps have endpoints removed, such as batch fetches and other users' playlists. Search is capped at 10 results per page.

steps.title: Add up to 5 users to the allowlist
steps.detail: In the app's Settings, open Users and Access and add each tester's name and the email address on their Spotify account.
actions: Settings → User Management / Users and Access
Add the name and Spotify email for each tester
steps.agentNote: An agent can add users once you've collected their emails.
steps.gotcha: The email must match the tester's Spotify account. Users who aren't on the list get 403 errors.

steps.title: Submit the Spotify Partner Application
steps.detail: Submit the Partner Application form linked from the quota modes page, using a company email address. You must meet the organization and 250k MAU criteria.
actions: Open the Partner Application link on the quota modes page
Submit company and product details from a company email address
steps.agentNote: An agent can draft answers. A person submits the form.
steps.gotcha: Spotify turns away individuals and pre-launch products.

steps.title: Request a quota extension in the Dashboard
steps.detail: Once your Partner Application is approved, open the app's Settings and go to the Quota extension Request tab. Complete the four-step questionnaire and submit. The app page then shows 'Sent'.
actions: Open the app, then Settings, then Quota extension Request
Complete the four-step questionnaire
Click Submit
steps.agentNote: An agent can fill in the questionnaire. A person reviews and submits it.

steps.title: Wait for Spotify's compliance review
steps.detail: Spotify checks the app against its Developer Policy and emails the result to the account address. The docs say this takes up to six weeks.
steps.gotcha: Spotify doesn't guarantee approval even when you meet the criteria.

blockers.symptom: 403 errors for users other than you
blockers.cause: The app is in development mode and the user isn't on the allowlist, or the 5-user cap is full.
blockers.fix: Add the user under Users and Access. To go past 5 users you need extended quota.

blockers.symptom: App suddenly stops working
blockers.cause: The owner's Premium subscription lapsed. Development-mode apps require it.
blockers.fix: Renew Premium on the owner account.

blockers.symptom: INVALID_CLIENT: Invalid redirect URI
blockers.cause: The redirect URI uses localhost, uses plain HTTP on a non-loopback host, or doesn't exactly match a registered URI.
blockers.fix: Register an exact HTTPS URI or a 127.0.0.1 or [::1] loopback URI.

blockers.symptom: Can't get extended quota as a solo developer or startup
blockers.cause: Since May 15, 2025, only registered businesses with at least 250k MAU are eligible.
blockers.fix: No workaround. Stay within 5 users, or apply once you meet the criteria.

blockers.symptom: Endpoints return errors or fields are missing in development mode
blockers.cause: The February 2026 changes removed batch endpoints, browse, other users' data and some response fields from development-mode apps.
blockers.fix: Use the replacement endpoints, such as /me/library and /items, or get extended quota.

unknowns.question: How long does the Partner Application take to process?
unknowns.why: The docs give six weeks for the quota review only. Nothing covers the Partner Application step.
unknowns.resolve: Ask in the Spotify for Developers community forum or contact Spotify partner support.

unknowns.question: Do restricted endpoints stay restricted for existing development-mode apps?
unknowns.why: A staff forum post reportedly postponed the endpoint changes for existing apps, but the migration guide doesn't mention a postponement.
unknowns.resolve: Check the February 2026 update thread on community.spotify.com and the migration guide's changelog.

summary: Any X user can connect as soon as you register an app in the X Developer Console, and the docs describe no app review. You must still buy prepaid pay-per-use credits, because new developers get no free tier and calls fail without a balance.

Complete the use-case profile

Buy an initial credit amount

Add scopes such as tweet.read, users.read and offline.access, plus tweet.write if you post

name: HubSpot
summary: You can create a HubSpot OAuth app and connect real customer accounts on the same day, but a marketplace-distribution app is capped at 25 installs until it is listed on the HubSpot Marketplace. Listing needs at least 3 active installs from production accounts not affiliated with you, live public URLs, and a review by HubSpot's Ecosystem Quality team. The first review takes up to 10 business days, and the full feedback process can run up to 60 days.
tierReason: Real customers can install an unlisted marketplace OAuth app today, after you sign the Acceptable Use Policy (AUP), but only up to 25 accounts until HubSpot approves a Marketplace listing.

composio.note: Composio has a managed HubSpot OAuth app, so you can prototype before you register your own. Register your own app before launch so your app's name is on the install screen and the 25-install cap and Marketplace listing are under your control.

totals.firstConnection: Today, in about 1 hour (in a developer test account or your own HubSpot account)

stages.whoCanConnect: Any HubSpot account, up to 25 installs (developer test accounts don't count). A super admin, or a user with the Marketplace access permission, does the install.
stages.userSees: An unverified-app warning until HubSpot's Ecosystem Quality team verifies the app
stages.unlock: Get 3 active installs from unaffiliated production accounts, then have HubSpot approve your Marketplace listing

stages.name: Listed on the Marketplace
stages.whoCanConnect: Any HubSpot account, with no install cap
stages.userSees: A normal install screen for a listed app

requirements.label: Redirect URI for your OAuth client
requirements.detail: The callback URL your OAuth client uses. You list it in `config.auth.redirectUrls`.

requirements.label: Signed Acceptable Use Policy
requirements.detail: Marketplace OAuth apps must sign the AUP before they can be installed in accounts that aren't developer test accounts.

requirements.label: 3 active installs from unaffiliated customers
requirements.detail: You need at least 3 unique HubSpot production accounts, not affiliated with you, with successful app activity in the past 30 days.

requirements.label: Live terms, privacy policy, support and pricing pages
requirements.detail: Your terms of service, privacy policy and support URLs must be live and public, and listed pricing must match your website. HubSpot checks the links with a crawler.

steps.detail: The initial review takes up to 10 business days. Rounds of feedback can stretch the full process to about 60 days after feedback is shared. Approval removes the 25-install cap automatically.
steps.gotcha: A listing can go back to draft without an email. Ask HubSpot support or the Ecosystem Quality team for the reason.

scopes.intro: Most CRM scopes (for example crm.objects.contacts.read/write) are self-serve: you declare them in app-hsmeta.json. Sensitive-data scopes need HubSpot's approval for public apps.

tiers.consequence: Public apps must request access from the Ecosystem Quality team, which allowlists the scope for testing and runs compliance checks before publishing. Existing users must reauthorize. Installing accounts need Enterprise.

blockers.symptom: Installs fail after the 25th account
blockers.cause: Marketplace-distribution apps on developer platform 2025.2 are capped at 25 installs until they are listed. HubSpot has enforced this since September 22, 2025.
blockers.fix: Get your Marketplace listing approved. HubSpot makes no exceptions, and the cap lifts automatically on approval. Migrated legacy apps already above 25 should file a support request.

blockers.symptom: Customers can't install the app outside test accounts
blockers.cause: The Acceptable Use Policy hasn't been signed, or the app uses private distribution and the account isn't on the allowlist.
blockers.fix: Sign the AUP on the Distribution tab, or add the account to the allowlist for private apps.

blockers.symptom: Listing review can't start: not enough installs
blockers.cause: Listing needs 3 active installs from unaffiliated production accounts.
blockers.fix: Use the 25-install allowance to onboard early customers first, then submit.

blockers.symptom: Listing sent back to draft
blockers.cause: Often broken or unreachable links, or the HubSpot crawler is blocked.
blockers.fix: Fix the URLs, allowlist the HubSpot Crawler, and ask Ecosystem Quality for the exact reason.

unknowns.why: The docs found focus on platform 2025.2 and only say that migrated apps get the cap.

unknowns.why: Docs say 'accounts'. One third-party blog says per portal but admits this isn't confirmed.
unknowns.resolve: Ask HubSpot developer support.

name: Zoom
summary: Your own Zoom account can connect within an hour of creating a General app in the Zoom App Marketplace. Before users outside your account can connect, the app has to pass Zoom's Marketplace review, which covers functionality, compliance and security. Forum reports put that at 2 to 12 weeks.
tierReason: An unpublished app can only be installed by your own Zoom account, plus a small approved beta group. Publishing it, even as unlisted, requires Zoom's functional and security review.

composio.note: Composio has a managed Zoom OAuth app, so you can prototype without passing Zoom's review yourself. Before launch, register and publish your own app so your name appears on the consent screen.

stages.name: Your Zoom account
stages.whoCanConnect: Users in your own Zoom account, through Local Test or the authorization URL
stages.userSees: The normal Zoom authorization screen for your unpublished app
stages.unlock: Complete the production build-flow requirements and ask Zoom to approve beta sharing outside your account

requirements.detail: You must be the account owner or an admin, or have the Zoom for developers role, to see the Develop menu in the Marketplace. On a free account, Zoom asks you to add a credit card or fill in a developer information form before you can submit for review.

requirements.label: Your redirect URI and allow-listed domain
requirements.detail: The build flow requires a development redirect URL and an OAuth allow list containing that URL or its base domain. Production needs its own redirect URL.

requirements.label: Privacy policy, terms, support and documentation pages on your own domain
requirements.detail: These pages must be hosted on a domain your company owns. Google Drive and Dropbox links are rejected. Your documentation must explain how to add the app, use it and remove it, including what happens to user data after removal.

requirements.label: A support page
requirements.detail: It should list support hours, a first-response SLA, and a way to open a case or email support.

requirements.label: A test plan and test accounts
requirements.detail: Give step-by-step testing instructions for each scope, as a document or a demo video. If your app needs specific data to test, include credentials for two user roles.

requirements.label: Technical design and security information
requirements.detail: In the build flow you describe your architecture, security controls and how you use scopes. Some developers report being asked for supporting evidence such as SSDLC documentation and SAST/DAST results.

requirements.label: Deauthorization handling
requirements.detail: Either use Zoom's standard removal flow, or handle the deauthorization event and call the token revoke endpoint.

Open Develop > Build App > General app
Name the app and choose User-managed or Admin-managed

blockers.symptom: Rejection asks for supporting evidence for the technical design

blockers.fix: Attach your security policy and testing evidence when you submit.

name: Pinterest
summary: Pinterest reviews your app twice. It approves a Trial request before you get credentials, and Trial limits Pins and boards you create to sandbox visibility under daily rate limits. For production you need Standard access, which takes a second review of a demo video showing your OAuth flow and a live API call.
tierReason: You only get an app secret after Pinterest manually approves Trial access, and you need a second, video-based review for Standard access before real users can use it in production.

composio.note: Composio lists Pinterest under Composio-managed OAuth, so you can prototype without waiting for Pinterest's Trial review. Register your own app before launch so your name is on the consent screen and you control your own access tier.

totals.firstConnection: After Pinterest approves your Trial request, which developers report takes from about 3 days to over 3 weeks

stages.name: Trial access

stages.userSees: Pinterest's standard OAuth consent page. Pins and boards created under Trial are visible only to their creator, as sandbox entities.

stages.whoCanConnect: Any Pinterest user. For apps registered on or after 2026-09-14, reading Pins or boards the authorizing account doesn't own needs separate Pinner data approval.
