requirements.label: Pinterest business account
requirements.detail: You administer the app from a business account with a verified email address. Apps linked to personal accounts disappear from the portal until you convert the account.

requirements.label: Public privacy policy on your company domain
requirements.detail: The privacy policy URL must be live, public and describe your app, and it must be on your company's domain. Otherwise the form rejects it with a company-name error.

requirements.label: Publicly accessible website
requirements.detail: Pinterest staff list a public site as a prerequisite for Trial access.

requirements.label: Demo video of the OAuth flow
requirements.detail: The video shows a user starting the connection in your app, Pinterest sign-in and consent, the return to your redirect URI, and a successful live API call. Terminal or Postman recordings are accepted.

steps.title: Sign in and accept the Developer Terms
steps.detail: Sign in with your business account and verify its email address. Then open My apps and accept the Developer Terms of Service.
actions: Create or convert to a Pinterest business account
Verify the account's email address
Open https://developers.pinterest.com/apps/ and accept the Developer Terms
steps.agentNote: A person must sign in and accept the terms. After that, an agent can fill in the app form.
steps.gotcha: Apps owned by a personal account stop appearing in the portal.

steps.title: Fill in the Connect app form
steps.detail: On My apps, choose Connect app and describe your app, use case and privacy policy URL. The app name needs at least 3 Latin letters or digits and can't contain "Pinterest".
actions: Select Connect app
Enter the app name, a specific description and the use case
Enter a privacy policy URL on your company domain
steps.agentNote: An agent can fill in the form. Hand back to the person to submit it.
steps.gotcha: Vague descriptions and privacy policy URLs off your company domain are the most common reasons Trial is denied or the form is rejected.

image.alt: My apps page with Connect app

steps.title: Submit the Trial access request
steps.detail: Submit the form to request Trial access. Pinterest emails you with its decision.
steps.gotcha: Denied requests have been reported to lock the app fields with no way to resubmit. If that happens, open a Help Center ticket.

steps.title: Wait for Trial approval
steps.detail: Pinterest publishes no turnaround time. Forum reports range from a few days to more than three weeks, and the app secret stays locked until approval.
steps.gotcha: Staff send pending-review questions to a known-issue support article instead of answering in the thread.

steps.title: Add your redirect URI
steps.detail: In My apps, choose Manage, open the Configure tab, enter your redirect URI under Redirect URIs, and select Add. It must match the redirect_uri you send exactly and must not redirect again.
actions: My apps > Manage > Configure
Redirect URIs: paste your redirect URI
Select Add
steps.agentNote: An agent can do this. A person copies the app secret into your OAuth client.
steps.gotcha: A mismatched trailing slash or protocol is the most common cause of authentication failures.

image.alt: Redirect URIs section on the Configure tab

steps.title: Configure your OAuth client
steps.detail: Copy the app ID and app secret into your OAuth client. Use https://www.pinterest.com/oauth/ to authorize, https://api.pinterest.com/v5/oauth/token to get tokens with HTTP Basic auth, and scopes such as boards:read and pins:write. Access tokens last 30 days, and refresh tokens last 60 days but renew continuously.
actions: Authorize URL: https://www.pinterest.com/oauth/ (response_type=code)
Token URL: https://api.pinterest.com/v5/oauth/token
Request only the scopes you need
Refresh tokens before they expire
steps.agentNote: An agent can enter the endpoint URLs and scopes. A person handles the app secret.
steps.gotcha: Apps created before 2025-09-25 must pass continuous_refresh=true.

steps.title: Test a connection with your own account
steps.detail: Run the OAuth flow with your business account and make a real API call. Under Trial, Pins and boards you create are sandbox entities visible only to you.
steps.agentNote: An agent can run the flow once a person is signed in to Pinterest.

steps.title: Record the demo video
steps.detail: Record a user starting the Pinterest connection in your app, signing in and approving, returning to your redirect URI, and completing a live API action.
steps.gotcha: Slides, mockups, generic product tours and demos without OAuth get denied.

steps.title: Submit the Standard access upgrade
steps.detail: On the app card in My apps, choose Upgrade. Verify the app info and privacy policy, upload the video and submit.
steps.gotcha: The Upgrade button appears only on apps that already have Trial access.

steps.title: Wait for the Standard access decision
steps.detail: Pinterest says it reviews upgrade requests regularly and emails you its decision. It gives no timeframe. To appeal a denial, use a Help Center ticket.

scopes.intro: Scopes use the {entity}:read or {entity}:write form. Pinterest doesn't classify them into review tiers, but newly registered apps need extra approval to read other people's Pins and boards.

tiers.grants: Read the authorizing user's boards, Pins and profile
tiers.consequence: Nothing beyond the Trial and Standard reviews.

tiers.grants: Create and edit boards and Pins
tiers.consequence: Created content is sandbox-only until you have Standard access.

tiers.grants: Access to secret boards and Pins
tiers.consequence: No separate review is documented. Request these only if you need them.

tiers.grants: Reading Pins and boards the authorizing account doesn't own
tiers.consequence: Apps registered on or after 2026-09-14 get 403 PINNER_DATA_ACCESS_DENIED unless Pinterest approves access through an account manager.

blockers.symptom: "Please include your company name in the URL for your privacy policy" when creating the app
blockers.cause: The privacy policy URL must be on your company's domain, and the check is strict.
blockers.fix: Host the policy on your own company domain. If it still fails, contact Pinterest support by private ticket or DM, because the usual ticket form needs an App ID.

blockers.symptom: App stuck in "Trial access pending" with the app secret locked
blockers.cause: Manual review backlog with no published turnaround time.
blockers.fix: Follow the community's known-issue article for pending Trial requests and file a Help Center ticket that includes your App ID.

blockers.symptom: HTTP 403 PINNER_DATA_ACCESS_DENIED when reading a board or Pin
blockers.cause: Apps registered on or after 2026-09-14 can only read the authorizing account's own Pins and boards without extra approval.
blockers.fix: Read only the authorizing user's own data, or ask your Pinterest account manager for Pinner data access. Don't retry in a loop.

blockers.symptom: Pins created through the API aren't visible to anyone else
blockers.cause: Under Trial access, Pins and boards are sandbox entities visible only to their creator.
blockers.fix: Upgrade to Standard access.

unknowns.question: Can Pinterest accounts other than yours authorize an app that only has Trial access?
unknowns.why: The access-tier, sandbox and FAQ pages don't say.
unknowns.resolve: After Trial approval, try the OAuth flow with a second business account, or ask in the Pinterest Business Community.

unknowns.question: How long does Standard access review take?
unknowns.why: Pinterest only says requests are reviewed regularly, and I found no dated reports from developers.
unknowns.resolve: Search community.pinterest.biz for recent upgrade-pending threads.

unknowns.question: What are the exact Trial rate limits?
unknowns.why: The docs say only that limits are daily per app. A third-party guide claims 1,000 requests per day, but no official source confirms it.
unknowns.resolve: Check the rate limits page on developers.pinterest.com or the response headers after you get Trial access.

unknowns.question: How do apps without an account manager get Pinner data access?
unknowns.why: The docs only point you to an account manager.
unknowns.resolve: Ask Pinterest developer support through the Help Center.

Run a test connection with your signed-in account

Accept the Developer Terms

Record the demo video

name: Monzo
summary: You can register a Monzo Developer API OAuth client in minutes and connect your own account the same day, but Monzo's docs say this API is not for public apps: it only connects your account and a small set of users you explicitly allow. To let any Monzo customer connect, you have to use Monzo's Open Banking APIs, which are only for FCA-licensed third-party providers (AISP/PISP) using certificates and dynamic client registration.
tierReason: Public access needs regulated status as an Account Information or Payment Initiation Service Provider under PSD2; the self-serve Developer API is limited to you and a few allowed users.

composio.note: Monzo isn't in Composio's managed-auth catalog, so plan to register your own Monzo OAuth client and pass its credentials to whatever OAuth client you use.

totals.firstConnection: Today, in about 15–30 minutes, for your own Monzo account through the Developer API

stages.name: Your own account
stages.whoCanConnect: Only the Monzo account that owns the OAuth client
stages.userSees: A Monzo email sign-in (magic link), then a push notification in the Monzo app asking them to approve access with PIN, fingerprint or Face ID
stages.unlock: Explicitly allow a small set of other users (the process isn't documented publicly)

stages.name: Allowed users
stages.whoCanConnect: A small set of Monzo users you explicitly allow
stages.userSees: Same email plus in-app approval flow. Users who aren't allowed get a 'Whoops! There was a problem' page after the magic link
stages.unlock: Become an FCA-authorised AISP/PISP (or use a licensed provider) and integrate Monzo's Open Banking APIs

stages.name: Open Banking (licensed TPP)
stages.whoCanConnect: Any Monzo customer, through the Open Banking consent flow
stages.userSees: An Open Banking consent screen, then approval in the Monzo app

requirements.label: A Monzo account with the Monzo app
requirements.detail: You sign in to the developer portal with your Monzo email and approve the login in the Monzo app. Community reports suggest business accounts may not be able to create clients.

requirements.label: A reachable redirect URI
requirements.detail: Your OAuth client needs a callback URL that receives the authorization code and state.

requirements.label: FCA authorisation as an AISP or PISP
requirements.detail: Monzo's Open Banking APIs are for licensed third-party providers only. In the EU you need eIDAS QWAC and QSealC certificates from a QTSP that Monzo trusts.

steps.title: Sign in to the Monzo developer portal
steps.detail: Go to developers.monzo.com, enter your Monzo email, click the magic link in the email, then approve the login in the Monzo app.
actions: Open developers.monzo.com and choose to sign in
Enter the email for your Monzo account and submit
Click 'Log Into Monzo' in the email
Approve the request in the Monzo app
steps.agentNote: A person has to sign in and approve in the Monzo app. Once you're signed in, an agent can continue.
steps.gotcha: The portal shows a 'not authorised' alert until you approve in the app.

steps.title: Create a confidential OAuth client
steps.detail: Open Clients and click '+ New OAuth Client'. Fill in Name, Logo URL (optional), Redirect URLs (your redirect URI) and Description, and set Confidentiality to Confidential so Monzo issues refresh tokens.
actions: Open Clients in the top-right menu
Click '+ New OAuth Client'
Name: something that identifies your project
Redirect URLs: your redirect URI
Confidentiality: Confidential
Submit
steps.agentNote: An agent can fill in and submit the form. It should stop before showing or copying the client secret.
steps.gotcha: Non-confidential clients get no refresh token, so users have to re-authenticate when the token expires (about 6 hours).

steps.title: Copy the client ID and secret into your OAuth client
steps.detail: Open the new client to see its Client ID and Client Secret. Store the secret in your OAuth client's configuration. The authorize URL is https://auth.monzo.com and the token endpoint is https://api.monzo.com/oauth2/token.
actions: Open the client entry
Copy the Client ID
Copy the Client Secret into secure storage
steps.agentNote: A person handles the secret. An agent can enter the client ID and endpoints.

steps.title: Connect and approve in the Monzo app
steps.detail: Run the authorization flow, then approve the push notification in the Monzo app. Until you approve it, the token has no permissions. Within 5 minutes, sync full transaction history, because after that only the last 90 days are available.
actions: Start the OAuth flow from your OAuth client
Click the email magic link
Approve the push notification in the Monzo app
Call /ping/whoami to confirm the token
steps.agentNote: An agent can start the flow and call /ping/whoami. A person has to approve in the app.
steps.gotcha: Each client holds only one active token per user. Getting a new token or refreshing invalidates the old one.

steps.title: Use Open Banking for public access
steps.detail: For any Monzo customer to connect, get FCA authorisation as an AISP/PISP (or use a licensed provider). Then register through Open Banking dynamic client registration (POST /register, tls_client_auth) and test in Monzo's sandbox.
actions: Obtain AISP/PISP authorisation
Get Open Banking (UK) or eIDAS QWAC/QSealC (EU) certificates
Register with POST /register using an SSA
Test in Monzo's Open Banking sandbox
steps.agentNote: Regulatory authorisation and certificates need a person. An agent can help with sandbox testing afterwards.
steps.gotcha: The Developer API client you created above can't be promoted to public use.

blockers.symptom: Other users see 'Whoops! There was a problem' after clicking the magic link
blockers.cause: The Developer API only allows your own account and users you explicitly allow
blockers.fix: Ask Monzo to allow the specific users, or move to Open Banking for public access

blockers.symptom: Token works but API calls return forbidden
blockers.cause: The user hasn't approved access in the Monzo app yet
blockers.fix: Have the user approve the push notification, then retry

blockers.symptom: Unable to create a new client in the portal
blockers.cause: Reported to be related to signing in with a business account
blockers.fix: Sign in with a personal Monzo account

unknowns.question: How do you explicitly allow other users on a Developer API client, and how many?
unknowns.why: The docs say 'a small set of users you explicitly allow' but don't describe a mechanism or a number
unknowns.resolve: Ask Monzo developer support or the Monzo developer community

unknowns.question: How long does FCA AISP/PISP authorisation take, and are there faster routes such as acting as an agent of a licensed provider?
unknowns.why: This is outside Monzo's docs
unknowns.resolve: See the FCA's payment services authorisation guidance, or consider an Open Banking aggregator

agentCan: Fill in the new OAuth client form
Enter your redirect URI, client ID and endpoints in your OAuth client
Start test flows and call /ping/whoami
youMust: Sign in with your Monzo email and approve in the Monzo app
Handle the client secret
Approve each connection in the Monzo app
Obtain FCA authorisation and certificates for public access

name: Mastodon
summary: Mastodon is self-serve: any app can register on any Mastodon server through a public API call, and there is no review, test-user list or user cap. The work is technical. Mastodon is decentralized, so you must register a separate OAuth client on each server your users come from, usually on the fly when a user enters their server domain.
tierReason: POST /api/v1/apps is a public endpoint that returns client credentials immediately, and the docs mention no app review or approval.

composio.note: Mastodon isn't in Composio's managed-auth catalog, managed or bring-your-own. Plan to register OAuth clients yourself on each Mastodon server.

stages.name: Your account
stages.whoCanConnect: You, on any Mastodon server where you've registered your app
stages.userSees: The server's standard authorization page, showing your app name and requested scopes
stages.unlock: Add per-server client registration so users on any server can connect

stages.name: Any Mastodon server
stages.whoCanConnect: Any user on any Mastodon server your app registers with
stages.userSees: The same authorization page on their own server. The docs describe no unverified-app warning.

requirements.label: A Mastodon account
requirements.detail: An account on any Mastodon server, used to test the authorization flow.

requirements.label: An absolute redirect URI
requirements.detail: A callback URL in your OAuth client. It must be absolute or the server returns 422. Use urn:ietf:wg:oauth:2.0:oob only for manual testing.

requirements.label: Per-server credential storage
requirements.detail: Somewhere to store an encrypted client_id and client_secret for each Mastodon server domain, so you register once per server and reuse the credentials.

steps.title: Choose the narrowest scopes
steps.detail: Pick granular scopes such as read:statuses or write:statuses, or the broad read, write and profile scopes. The scopes you register are the most an authorize request can ask for. Avoid follow (deprecated since 3.5.0) and crypto (removed in 4.3.0).
actions: List the API calls your integration makes
Map them to scopes (e.g. read:accounts, write:statuses, write:media)
Add profile if you only need the user's identity (4.3.0+)
steps.agentNote: An agent can map the features to scopes from the scopes doc.
steps.gotcha: Asking for a scope at authorize time that you didn't register makes the authorization fail.

steps.title: Register your app on a Mastodon server
steps.detail: Send POST https://{server}/api/v1/apps with client_name, redirect_uris, scopes (space-separated) and an optional website. No auth is needed. The response contains client_id and client_secret.
actions: POST /api/v1/apps with client_name, redirect_uris (your redirect URI), scopes and website
Hand the client_id and client_secret to your backend's secret store without displaying them
steps.agentNote: An agent can make the call. A person or your backend should handle and store the client_secret.
steps.gotcha: Before 4.3, servers could delete apps that were registered but never used. On older servers, request a client_credentials token right after registering to keep the app active.

steps.title: Configure your OAuth client endpoints
steps.detail: Set the authorize URL to https://{server}/oauth/authorize and the token URL to https://{server}/oauth/token, with response_type=code. Use PKCE (S256 only) on servers running 4.3.0 or later.
actions: Set authorize URL and token URL for the server
Set scope to a subset of the registered scopes
Enable PKCE S256 if GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server returns 200
steps.agentNote: An agent can set up the client config. The client_secret should be loaded from your secret store, not pasted by the agent.
steps.gotcha: Very long state values can break Doorkeeper redirects. Keep state short and store the rest on your server.

steps.title: Connect your own account and verify
steps.detail: Sign in on your server, approve the app, and exchange the code for a token. Call GET /api/v1/accounts/verify_credentials to confirm the token works.
actions: Open the authorize URL and approve
Exchange the code at /oauth/token (a code works only once)
Call /api/v1/accounts/verify_credentials
steps.agentNote: The person signs in and approves. An agent can then run the verification call.
steps.gotcha: invalid_grant usually means the redirect_uri doesn't match exactly, or the code came from a client registered on another server.

steps.title: Register automatically for each user's server
steps.detail: Ask users for their server domain, look up stored credentials for that domain, and call POST /api/v1/apps if none exist. Route authorize and token requests to that server.
actions: Add a server-domain input to your connect flow
Cache client credentials per domain, encrypted
Use the discovery endpoint to detect PKCE and scope support, falling back if it returns 404 (pre-4.3)
steps.agentNote: An agent can implement and test this logic.
steps.gotcha: Mastodon doesn't support standard RFC 7591 Dynamic Client Registration, so generic DCR clients won't work. Use /api/v1/apps.

scopes.intro: Mastodon has no scope review. Every scope is self-serve, but admin scopes only work for accounts with moderator or admin roles on that server.

tiers.grants: The user's identity, plus reading and writing their data
tiers.consequence: Nothing. Available immediately.

tiers.grants: Moderation and admin APIs
tiers.consequence: No review, but only usable by staff accounts on that server

blockers.symptom: 422 Redirect URI must be an absolute URI
blockers.cause: The redirect URI passed to /api/v1/apps is relative or malformed.
blockers.fix: Register a full absolute URL, or urn:ietf:wg:oauth:2.0:oob for testing.

blockers.symptom: invalid_grant at token exchange
blockers.cause: The redirect_uri doesn't match the registered one, or the client_id belongs to a different server.
blockers.fix: Use the exact registered redirect URI and the credentials stored for that server's domain.

blockers.symptom: Discovery endpoint returns 404
blockers.cause: The server runs a Mastodon version before 4.3.0, which has no discovery endpoint and no PKCE.
blockers.fix: Fall back to the plain authorization code flow without PKCE and register only scopes that server supports.

blockers.symptom: 429 Too Many Requests
blockers.cause: The default limit is 300 calls per 5 minutes per account and per IP. Media uploads are limited to 30 per 30 minutes.
blockers.fix: Respect the X-RateLimit headers and back off.

unknowns.question: Can individual server admins block or remove third-party apps, or restrict registration through /api/v1/apps?
unknowns.why: The official docs don't cover admin controls over third-party apps.
unknowns.resolve: Check the server's rules or ask its admins. Test registration on the major servers your users are on.

unknowns.question: Is POST /api/v1/apps rate-limited by IP?
unknowns.why: The rate limits page doesn't list a separate limit for app registration.
unknowns.resolve: Watch the X-RateLimit headers when registering, and cache credentials so you register once per server.

unknowns.question: Do Mastodon-compatible servers (forks or other ActivityPub software) behave the same way?
unknowns.why: This research covered upstream Mastodon only.
unknowns.resolve: Test against each server type your users need.

agentCan: Choose scopes
Call POST /api/v1/apps on a server
Configure the authorize and token URLs and PKCE in your OAuth client
Implement per-server registration and credential caching
Run verify_credentials after you connect
youMust: Have a Mastodon account and sign in to approve the test connection
Store the client_secret for each server securely
Decide which servers or server types to support

name: WeChat
summary: Getting to public launch is hard. You must register a company with the WeChat Open Platform (open.weixin.qq.com), pay for developer verification and pass a manual review of your website app, and until that review passes, not even your own account can connect.
tierReason: WeChat Login for websites requires paid developer verification that individuals reportedly can't get, plus a manual app review before any account can connect.

composio.note: WeChat isn't in Composio's managed-auth or bring-your-own lists (checked 2026-10-27), so expect to register your own Open Platform app and use it with whatever OAuth client you choose.

totals.firstConnection: Only after developer verification and website app review both pass, roughly 1 to 2 weeks according to developer reports

stages.name: Approved website app
stages.whoCanConnect: No one until the app is approved. After that, any WeChat user who scans the QR code.
stages.userSees: Before approval, the QR login page fails with errors (scope or redirect errors). After approval, users see the WeChat QR code login page with your app name.
stages.unlock: Once the website app is approved and its WeChat Login interface shows as granted, the same app works for every user. There is no separate launch review.

stages.name: Public launch
stages.whoCanConnect: Any WeChat user
stages.userSees: The WeChat QR code login (scope snsapi_login), confirmed on their phone

requirements.label: WeChat Open Platform developer account
requirements.detail: Register at open.weixin.qq.com with an email address that isn't used by any other WeChat platform account.

requirements.label: Registered company or organization
requirements.detail: Developers report that developer verification takes only enterprise, government or organization materials, not individuals. Mainland verification reportedly needs the legal representative's face scan and a corporate bank account.

requirements.label: Developer verification fee
requirements.detail: Reported as 300 CNY for mainland entities and 99 USD for overseas entities, charged yearly and not refundable.

requirements.label: Live website and callback domain
requirements.detail: You need a working website and the domain where your redirect URI lives. Your redirect_uri must be on the authorization callback domain you declared during review.

requirements.label: Signed website information registration form
requirements.detail: Submit the 微信开放平台网站信息登记表 (website information registration form). The app name on it must match the app name you enter. If the site's operator differs from the verified entity, you also need an authorization letter.

steps.title: Register a WeChat Open Platform account
steps.detail: Sign up at open.weixin.qq.com with an email address and activate the account. Each WeChat platform (Official Accounts, Mini Programs, Open Platform) needs its own email address.
actions: Go to open.weixin.qq.com and choose to register
Use an email address not tied to another WeChat platform account
Confirm the activation email and bind an administrator WeChat account
steps.agentNote: A person has to sign up and scan QR codes with their phone. An agent can fill in profile fields once signed in.
steps.gotcha: An email address already used for an Official Account or Mini Program can't be reused here.

steps.title: Apply for developer verification and pay
steps.detail: In Account Center, open 开发者资质认证 (developer verification). Accept the agreement, submit your company documents, enter invoice details and pay the fee.
actions: Account Center > 开发者资质认证
Accept the service agreement
Upload business license and entity details, then complete the legal representative and corporate bank checks
Enter invoice details and pay (reported as 300 CNY, or 99 USD overseas)
steps.agentNote: An agent can fill in text fields. Payment, identity checks and document uploads need a person.
steps.gotcha: Individual-type accounts can't complete this step. The fee is reportedly not refunded if you're rejected.

steps.title: Wait for verification approval
steps.detail: Tencent reviews your verification. Developers report 1 to 3 days, and some report about a week.
steps.gotcha: Incomplete materials send you back through review. Submit everything the first time.

steps.title: Create a website app
steps.detail: In 管理中心 (Management Center) > 网站应用 (website apps), click 创建网站应用 (create website app). Enter the basic info and website info, including app name, logo, website URL and the authorization callback domain, then upload the signed website information registration form.
actions: Management Center > 网站应用 > 创建网站应用
Fill in basic info: app name, description, logo
Fill in website info: website URL and authorization callback domain (domain only, e.g. www.example.com, no scheme or path)
Upload the signed website information registration form
Submit for review
steps.agentNote: An agent can fill in the form fields and the callback domain. A person should sign the registration form, upload it and submit.
steps.gotcha: Enter only the domain for the callback domain. The app name must exactly match the name on the registration form, or the review is rejected.

steps.title: Wait for website app review
steps.detail: Tencent reviews the website app. Developers report up to about 7 days. Some say verification and app creation can run in parallel.
steps.gotcha: A rejection restarts the review clock.

steps.title: Confirm WeChat Login is granted
steps.detail: Open the approved app. Check that 微信登录 (WeChat Login) shows as granted under 接口信息 (interface info), and note the AppID.
actions: Open the app from the 网站应用 list
Check that 接口信息 > 微信登录 is granted
Copy the AppID
steps.agentNote: An agent can check the status and copy the AppID. A person should reveal the AppSecret and put it in your OAuth client's secret store.
steps.gotcha: If WeChat Login isn't granted, authorization fails with a scope error.

steps.title: Store the AppSecret in your OAuth client
steps.detail: Generate or reveal the AppSecret. Store it server-side in your OAuth client, since the token exchange at api.weixin.qq.com/sns/oauth2/access_token needs it.
actions: Reveal the AppSecret (this needs administrator QR confirmation)
Save it in your OAuth client's secret storage
steps.agentNote: A person handles this step. Don't give the secret to an agent.
steps.gotcha: Never put the AppSecret in front-end code.

steps.title: Configure your OAuth client endpoints
steps.detail: Set the authorize URL to https://open.weixin.qq.com/connect/qrconnect with appid, a URL-encoded redirect_uri, response_type=code, scope=snsapi_login and state. The token URL is https://api.weixin.qq.com/sns/oauth2/access_token, which takes appid, secret, code and grant_type=authorization_code.
actions: Authorize URL: https://open.weixin.qq.com/connect/qrconnect
Token URL: https://api.weixin.qq.com/sns/oauth2/access_token
Scope: snsapi_login
Make sure your redirect URI is on the approved callback domain
steps.agentNote: An agent can enter the endpoints and the redirect URI and run a test login. A person scans the QR code.
steps.gotcha: WeChat uses non-standard parameter names (appid and secret instead of client_id and client_secret), so generic OAuth clients often need custom configuration. Codes expire in 10 minutes and access tokens in 2 hours.

scopes.intro: Website apps use a single scope. Getting it depends on the app approval, not on a per-scope review.

tiers.grants: QR code login. Returns the openid (plus a unionid if bound), and the token can be used to fetch basic profile info.
tiers.consequence: Available only after developer verification and website app approval

blockers.symptom: Developer verification can't be submitted, or is rejected, for an individual account
blockers.cause: Developers report that verification requires enterprise or organization materials.

name: Zendesk
summary: You can create a local OAuth client and connect your own Zendesk instance in under an hour, but that client only works on one subdomain. To let other Zendesk customers connect, Zendesk has to approve a global OAuth client, and since August 2025 your integration must also go through Marketplace review (1 to 3 weeks for new submissions), even if it won't be listed publicly.
tierReason: Third-party integrations must use a Zendesk-approved global OAuth client and pass Marketplace review. Local clients only work on one instance, and you're not allowed to use a customer's own OAuth client or API token.

composio.note: Composio lists a managed Zendesk OAuth app, so you can prototype without registering your own client. To ship under your own name and meet Zendesk's Marketplace rules (approved global client plus marketplace headers), register your own global client before launch.

totals.firstConnection: Today, in about 30 minutes, on your own Zendesk subdomain using a local OAuth client

stages.name: Your instance
stages.whoCanConnect: Only users on the single Zendesk subdomain where you created the local OAuth client
stages.userSees: The Zendesk authorization page on your subdomain, showing your client name, logo and requested scopes
stages.unlock: Zendesk approves your global OAuth request and accepts your Marketplace integration submission

stages.name: Any Zendesk customer
stages.whoCanConnect: Admins and users on any Zendesk subdomain
stages.userSees: The Zendesk authorization page on their own subdomain, listing only the scopes Zendesk allowed for your global client

requirements.label: Zendesk account with admin access
requirements.detail: You need admin rights in Admin Center to create OAuth clients. A free 14-day Support trial works for building.

requirements.label: Sponsored developer account with a d3v- subdomain
requirements.detail: Global OAuth requests are only accepted from subdomains that start with d3v-. You get one by renaming a trial subdomain and filling in Zendesk's Sponsored Account Request Form. It's free, covers 5 agents, and must not be used for real support.

requirements.label: Organization registered on the Marketplace portal
requirements.detail: Register your organization at apps.zendesk.com. You need it to request a global client, to claim it, to submit the app, and to get the organization ID header value.

requirements.label: Privacy notice
requirements.detail: Under the Zendesk Developer Terms, you must publish a privacy notice that discloses what data your integration accesses, uses and stores, and why.

requirements.label: HTTPS redirect URI
requirements.detail: Redirect URLs must be absolute and use HTTPS. The only exceptions are localhost and 127.0.0.1.

steps.title: Create a local OAuth client in Admin Center
steps.detail: In Admin Center, go to Apps and integrations > APIs > OAuth clients and click Add OAuth client. If you'll request a global client later, do this on your d3v- account and fill in every field.
actions: Name: your product name (users see it on the consent page)
Description, Company, Logo (JPG/GIF/PNG): fill these in, because they're mandatory for global requests
Identifier: prefix it with zdg- (for example zdg-yourproduct). This becomes your client_id
Client kind: Confidential for a backend that holds a secret, or Public if you use PKCE only
Redirect URLs: your redirect URI, one per line
Scopes: list only what you need (for example tickets:read tickets:write), or leave empty to allow all
Click Save
steps.agentNote: An agent can fill the form once an admin is signed in. Stop before the secret appears after Save and hand off to a person.
steps.gotcha: A local client works only on the subdomain where you created it. Every authorization and token URL includes the user's subdomain.

link.label: Zendesk Admin Center OAuth clients (help article)

steps.title: Copy the client secret and store it securely
steps.detail: After the first Save, a Secret field appears. Zendesk shows the full secret only once and later shows only the first nine characters. Copy it into your secrets store and click Save again.
actions: Copy the secret into your secret manager
Click Save again to finish
steps.agentNote: A person must handle the secret.
steps.gotcha: Keep the secret. Once the client becomes global, you lose access to its admin page, and you'll need the first 6 characters of the secret to claim the client.

steps.title: Configure your OAuth client and test a connection
steps.detail: Point your OAuth client at https://{subdomain}.zendesk.com/oauth/authorizations/new and https://{subdomain}.zendesk.com/oauth/tokens. Ask each user for their subdomain before you start the flow. Support refresh tokens: access tokens last 30 minutes and refresh tokens 30 days by default, and each refresh rotates both.
actions: Set the authorization URL to https://{subdomain}.zendesk.com/oauth/authorizations/new with response_type=code, client_id, redirect_uri, scope and state
Set the token URL to https://{subdomain}.zendesk.com/oauth/tokens (grant_type=authorization_code, then refresh_token)
For PKCE, send code_challenge with code_challenge_method=S256, then send code_verifier
Exchange the code within 120 seconds
Connect your own instance and make a test API call
steps.agentNote: An agent can enter the endpoints, client_id and redirect URI and run the test. A person enters the secret.
steps.gotcha: Refreshing invalidates the previous access and refresh tokens. Store the new pair every time, or users will have to authorize again.

steps.title: Get a sponsored d3v- developer account
steps.detail: Start a Zendesk Support trial, rename the subdomain so it starts with d3v-, and submit the Sponsored Account Request Form. Zendesk emails you when the trial is converted.
actions: Sign up at zendesk.com/register/free-trial
Rename the subdomain with the d3v- prefix
Submit the form at https://forms.gle/NDkrqK9xkZrnWoyk9
steps.agentNote: A person must sign up and submit the form.
steps.gotcha: Zendesk suspends sponsored accounts that are used for real customer support.

link.label: Getting a trial or sponsored account

steps.title: Wait for sponsored account conversion
steps.detail: Zendesk converts the trial to a sponsored account and notifies you. The docs don't give a timeline.
steps.gotcha: A trial expires after 14 days, so submit the form early.

steps.title: Register your organization on the Marketplace portal
steps.detail: Sign in at apps.zendesk.com and register your organization. Your organization ID, shown at the top of the Organization page, is the value for the X-Zendesk-Marketplace-Organization-Id header.
actions: Sign in at apps.zendesk.com
Register the organization and accept the developer terms
Note the organization ID
steps.agentNote: A person must accept the terms. An agent can then read off the organization ID.

steps.title: Request a global OAuth client
steps.detail: In the Marketplace portal, choose Global OAuth > Request new OAuth. The d3v- subdomain and zdg- identifier are prefilled; check that they match your local client and request only the scopes you need.
actions: Open Global OAuth in the left menu
Click Request new OAuth
Confirm the d3v- subdomain and zdg- identifier
List the minimum scopes
Submit, then add support@appsubmission.zendesk.com to your contacts
steps.agentNote: An agent can fill the form. A person should review the scopes and submit.
steps.gotcha: Zendesk rejects requests from subdomains without the d3v- prefix, and requests where the local client's optional fields are blank.

link.label: Set up a global OAuth client

image.alt: Global OAuth request form in the Zendesk Marketplace portal

steps.title: Wait for global OAuth approval
steps.detail: You get an email and a ticket reference. If Zendesk approves, it converts your local client into a global client, possibly with a restricted set of allowed scopes. The docs give no timeframe.
steps.gotcha: After conversion, only Zendesk's Marketplace Operations team can edit the client. To change scopes, contact Zendesk Support and mention "global oauth allowed scopes" and your client_id.

steps.title: Claim the global client in the portal
steps.detail: In the Global OAuth section, click Claim Global Auth. Enter the client_id and the first 6 characters of the client secret so the client is linked to your organization.
actions: Click Claim Global Auth
Enter the OAuth identifier and the first 6 characters of the secret
Click Claim
steps.agentNote: Part of the secret is involved, so a person should do this.

image.alt: Claim a global OAuth client dialog

steps.title: Submit your integration app to the Marketplace
steps.detail: Submit an integration app: a ZIP with marketing assets, translations and a manifest that sets "marketingOnly": true. On the Compliance tab, answer Yes to using a global OAuth client and select your claimed client. Designate a test account where Zendesk can verify your headers.
actions: Prepare the ZIP with manifest (marketingOnly: true), translations and assets
Fill in the listing, including a privacy policy URL
On Compliance, answer Yes to the global OAuth question and select your client
Designate a test account for header verification
steps.agentNote: An agent can prepare the assets and fill in the fields. A person must submit.
steps.gotcha: Integrations that aren't publicly listed must also create a Marketplace profile and submit.

image.alt: App submission compliance questions including global OAuth client selection

steps.title: Add the Marketplace headers to API calls
steps.detail: Send X-Zendesk-Marketplace-Name, X-Zendesk-Marketplace-Organization-Id and X-Zendesk-Marketplace-App-Id on every Zendesk API request your servers make. Zendesk assigns the app ID when you submit, so update your code then.
actions: Add the three headers to your API request code
Make calls against the designated test account so Zendesk can see the headers
steps.agentNote: An agent can update the request configuration and run test calls.
steps.gotcha: Zendesk won't approve the app until it sees these headers on your test account.

steps.title: Wait for Marketplace review
steps.detail: Zendesk says new submissions take 1 to 3 weeks and updates take 1 to 2 weeks.

scopes.intro: Zendesk doesn't classify scopes as sensitive or restricted. For a global client, Zendesk may cap the allowed scopes when it approves your request. Requesting a scope outside that list fails with invalid_scope.

tiers.grants: Read or write access to all resources
tiers.consequence: Zendesk reviews these as part of the global OAuth request, which asks for the minimum scopes your app needs

tiers.grants: Access to a single resource type
tiers.consequence: Nothing extra. These are preferred for a narrow request

tiers.grants: Lets admins act on behalf of end users
tiers.consequence: No separate process is documented. It's listed in the global request like any other scope (inferred)

blockers.symptom: Global OAuth request is rejected or not accepted
blockers.cause: The request was submitted from a subdomain without the d3v- prefix, or the local client's identifier lacks zdg- or has empty optional fields
blockers.fix: Get a sponsored d3v- account, recreate the local client with a zdg- identifier and every field filled in, then resubmit

blockers.symptom: OAuth fails for customers on other subdomains
blockers.cause: Local OAuth clients only exist on the instance where they were created
blockers.fix: Use an approved global OAuth client. Don't ask customers to create their own clients or API tokens, which Zendesk prohibits for third parties

blockers.symptom: 400 Bad Request with invalid_scope
blockers.cause: Your app requested a scope outside the allowed scopes Zendesk set on the global client
blockers.fix: Request only allowed scopes, or contact Zendesk Support about "global oauth allowed scopes" with your client_id

blockers.symptom: 401 invalid_token after about 30 minutes
blockers.cause: Access tokens expire by default: refresh tokens are required for global clients since February 2, 2026, and default expiry applies to local clients created after April 30, 2026
blockers.fix: Implement the refresh_token grant and store the rotated tokens each time

blockers.symptom: Marketplace submission stalls
blockers.cause: Zendesk doesn't see the X-Zendesk-Marketplace-* headers on the designated test account
blockers.fix: Add all three headers once the app ID is assigned and make API calls against the test account

unknowns.question: How long does global OAuth client approval take?
unknowns.why: Zendesk's docs and third-party guides give no timeframe, and no community reports turned up
unknowns.resolve: Watch the ticket Zendesk sends after you submit, or ask in Zendesk's developer community

unknowns.question: How long does sponsored account conversion take?
unknowns.why: The docs only say Zendesk will notify you
unknowns.resolve: Submit the form early, while your trial still has time left

unknowns.question: Must the global OAuth request be approved before you submit the Marketplace app, or can they run in parallel?
unknowns.why: The docs describe both steps but don't say which order is required
unknowns.resolve: Ask Marketplace Operations in the global OAuth ticket

unknowns.question: What exactly is required for an unlisted (private distribution) integration?
unknowns.why: The developer update says unlisted integrations must submit, but no page details how unlisted listings work
unknowns.resolve: Check the Marketplace portal submission options or ask Zendesk partner support

Test a connection against your own instance
Fill in the global OAuth request and app submission forms for review
Add the X-Zendesk-Marketplace-* headers to API calls and run test calls

name: GitHub
summary: GitHub is self-serve: you register an OAuth app in Developer settings in a few minutes, and anyone can connect right away. GitHub doesn't review apps or scopes. The main hurdle is on the customer side: organizations can require an owner to approve your app before it can reach their private data.
tierReason: Any GitHub account can create an OAuth app and get a client ID and secret immediately, and GitHub's docs describe no app review, verification or user cap.

composio.note: Composio has a managed GitHub OAuth app, so you can prototype without registering your own. Register your own before launch so your app's name appears on GitHub's consent screen and in organization approval requests.

stages.name: Your account
stages.whoCanConnect: You, as soon as the app is registered
stages.userSees: GitHub's authorization page, showing your app name and the scopes you request
stages.unlock: Nothing. The same app already works for any GitHub user.

stages.name: Public launch
stages.whoCanConnect: Any GitHub user. To reach private data in an organization that restricts OAuth apps, an owner of that organization must approve your app first.
stages.userSees: The same authorization page. In restricted organizations, the user sees the option to request owner approval.

requirements.label: A GitHub account or organization to own the app
requirements.detail: A personal account or an organization can own up to 100 OAuth apps. For production, register the app under an organization so it doesn't depend on one person.

requirements.label: Homepage URL and redirect URI
requirements.detail: You need a public homepage URL and the redirect URI from your OAuth client. GitHub accepts up to 10 callback URLs per app.

steps.title: Open OAuth apps in Developer settings
steps.detail: Sign in to GitHub, then go to Settings > Developer settings > OAuth apps. For an organization-owned app, open the organization's Settings > Developer settings instead.
actions: Sign in to github.com
Click your profile picture > Settings > Developer settings > OAuth apps
Click New OAuth App (or Register a new application)
steps.agentNote: Once you're signed in, an agent can navigate here.
steps.gotcha: Choose the owner carefully. An app registered under a personal account depends on that person's account until you transfer it.

steps.title: Fill in the OAuth app form
steps.detail: Enter the application name, homepage URL, an optional description and your redirect URI as the Authorization callback URL. Leave Device Flow off unless you need it.
actions: Application name: the public name users will see
Homepage URL: your product's website
Application description (optional)
Authorization callback URL: your redirect URI (use Add callback URL for more, up to 10)
Expire user access tokens: on by default. Turn it off only if your OAuth client can't refresh tokens.
Click Register application
steps.agentNote: An agent can fill in the whole form. Copy the redirect URI exactly from your OAuth client's configuration.
steps.gotcha: By default, the redirect URI must match a registered callback exactly. With expiring tokens on, access tokens last 8 hours, so your OAuth client must store and use refresh tokens.

steps.title: Generate and store the client secret
steps.detail: On the app page, copy the Client ID and click Generate a new client secret. Put the ID and secret into your OAuth client's configuration yourself.
actions: Copy the Client ID
Click Generate a new client secret and copy it immediately
Enter both in your OAuth client (your backend, Composio, Nango or another client)
steps.agentNote: An agent can copy the Client ID. A person should handle the client secret.
steps.gotcha: GitHub shows the secret only once. If you lose it, generate a new one.

steps.title: Configure endpoints and scopes in your client
steps.detail: Set the authorize URL to https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize and the token URL to https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token. Request only the scopes you need, such as read:user, user:email, repo or read:org.
actions: Authorize URL: https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize
Token URL: https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token
Scopes: space-separated, for example 'read:user user:email repo'
Handle refresh with grant_type=refresh_token if expiring tokens are on
steps.agentNote: An agent can set the non-secret fields and scopes.
steps.gotcha: Users can reduce the scopes they grant. Read the granted scopes from the token response and don't assume they match what you requested.

steps.title: Connect your own GitHub account
steps.detail: Run the authorization flow with your account and call an API endpoint such as GET /user. Also test with a repository in an organization to check the org-approval path.
actions: Start the flow from your OAuth client
Approve on GitHub's consent page
Call the API with the token
steps.agentNote: An agent can drive the test. A person may need to sign in and approve.
steps.gotcha: GitHub allows 10 tokens per user/app/scope combination. Creating more revokes older tokens, and token creation is limited to 10 per hour, so repeated tests can invalidate earlier tokens.

steps.title: Tell users how to get org owner approval
steps.detail: New organizations restrict OAuth apps by default. Add help text telling users to request approval during authorization and to ask an organization owner to approve your app.
actions: Add a help page explaining how to request organization approval
Show a clear message when the API returns 403 or missing org repositories
steps.agentNote: An agent can draft the help text. Approval itself happens in each customer's organization.
steps.gotcha: If users skip the org request on first authorization, they have to request access from their authorized OAuth apps settings, or revoke and re-authorize.

blockers.symptom: Organization private repositories are missing, or API calls return 403 mentioning OAuth App access restrictions
blockers.cause: The organization has OAuth app access restrictions on, which is the default for new organizations, and no owner has approved your app.
blockers.fix: Have the user request approval for your app, and have an organization owner approve it in the organization's third-party access settings. Then re-check access.

blockers.symptom: redirect_uri mismatch error on GitHub's authorization page
blockers.cause: The redirect URI your OAuth client sends doesn't exactly match a registered callback URL.
blockers.fix: Add your client's exact redirect URI as a callback URL in the app settings. You can register up to 10.

blockers.symptom: Earlier tokens stop working, or users are asked to re-authorize
blockers.cause: GitHub keeps at most 10 tokens per user/app/scope combination and limits token creation to 10 per hour. Refresh tokens expire after 6 months without use.
blockers.fix: Reuse stored tokens rather than re-running the flow, and refresh tokens before they lapse.

unknowns.question: Should you build a GitHub App instead of an OAuth app?
unknowns.why: This research covered OAuth apps only. GitHub Apps use fine-grained permissions instead of scopes and have their own installation flow.
unknowns.resolve: Read GitHub's docs comparing GitHub Apps and OAuth apps, and choose based on whether you need per-repository installs and fine-grained permissions.

unknowns.question: Is GitHub Marketplace listing needed for anything beyond discovery or billing?
unknowns.why: Marketplace wasn't researched. It isn't required for users to authorize an OAuth app.
unknowns.resolve: Check GitHub's Marketplace docs if you want a listing or paid plans through GitHub.

Copy the Client ID and set the endpoints and scopes in your OAuth client
Run a test connection and check the granted scopes
Draft help text for organization approval

Generate the client secret and store it in your OAuth client
Ask organization owners to approve the app where restrictions apply
